articles.title: Report: US intelligence fears China could access F-35 technology in $24B Saudi deal
articles.body:
U.S. intelligence officials have raised concerns that a proposed $24 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia could expose some of the aircraft’s most sensitive technology to Chinese espionage, The New York Times reported, citing American officials familiar with internal assessments.
The planned package includes 48 F-35s and a spare engine. President Donald Trump announced the sale in November 2025, a day before hosting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman at the White House. The deal has since moved forward, with the State Department sending it to two congressional committees in June for informal approval.
According to the Times, intelligence analysts have warned that China could potentially gain access to F-35 technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or through the kingdom’s expanding military and security relationship with Beijing.
A recent Defense Intelligence Agency report examined Chinese military access to Saudi bases and the kingdom’s use of Chinese telecommunications equipment. It also questioned whether U.S. and Saudi officials could adequately secure sites housing sensitive F-35 systems.
Pentagon officials are particularly concerned about protecting the jet’s advanced radar and surveillance technology. The report also raised questions over whether Riyadh would agree to limit contact between Chinese military or intelligence personnel and facilities connected to the aircraft.
Another concern is the presence of equipment made by Chinese telecommunications giants Huawei and ZTE. U.S. intelligence officials have asked whether Saudi Arabia would be willing to remove such technology from communications infrastructure and defense installations tied to the F-35 program.
The warnings echo concerns raised during Trump’s first term, when Washington agreed to sell F-35s to the United Arab Emirates after Abu Dhabi normalized relations with Israel in 2020. That deal was later reviewed as the UAE strengthened military, intelligence and technology ties with China, and the sales process was ultimately halted.
Saudi Arabia has long been one of the largest buyers of U.S. weapons, but it also maintains significant defense ties with Beijing. The kingdom purchases ballistic missiles from China, while the Chinese military has helped Saudi Arabia develop missile production facilities and improve its missile capabilities, according to the Times.
The proposed F-35 sale has also raised concerns in Israel, the only country in the Middle East that currently operates the aircraft. U.S. law requires Washington to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge in the region when approving major weapons sales to neighboring states.
Previous U.S. administrations conducted lengthy classified reviews to determine whether arms sales could undermine that advantage. Some Israeli officials have expressed reservations about the Saudi deal, as they did over the proposed sale to the UAE.
The Saudi military, meanwhile, has faced growing pressure to improve its capabilities. Crown Prince Mohammed has sought for years to acquire F-35s, and the kingdom’s armed forces have struggled to defend against attacks from Iran during the current U.S.-Israeli war with Tehran, the Times reported. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis has also resumed.
Congress could still complicate the deal. Lawmakers and aides have been pressing the administration over the intelligence warnings, according to the report.
The sale also comes as Trump has agreed to help Saudi Arabia develop a civilian nuclear program, another initiative that has prompted security concerns because the crown prince has said Riyadh would seek nuclear weapons if Iran obtained them.

articles.title: Germany’s rearmament push runs through America
articles.body:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stands alongside German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius during an honor cordon welcome ceremony at the Pentagon in Washington on Sept. 15, 2026. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images
WASHINGTON — German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius came to the Pentagon on Wednesday with a dilemma: Berlin wants a stronger, more self-reliant European military, but much of what it needs comes from the United States.
Pistorius is in the U.S. this week after earlier being rebuffed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Berlin is seeking direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.
"Germany is strengthening its defense capabilities and acts as a driving force in Europe," Pistorius said at the Pentagon alongside Hegseth. "We Europeans want to take some of the burden off the U.S. and assume primary responsibility for conventional deterrence in Europe over time."
Advertisement
He said Germany has increased its defense spending to $147 billion this year — up by 25% compared to 2025 — and has almost tripled it over the last decade.
The two signed a statement of intent on defense-industrial cooperation covering joint production, licensed manufacturing, maintenance hubs and supply-chain resilience. What the document did not contain were concrete projects, timelines or investment commitments.
Despite efforts by Germany and other European countries to build up their defense industries and reduce dependence on the U.S. in areas such as long-range missiles and satellites, much of the new defense spending is ending up with American companies.
On Friday, Pistorius will travel to Fort Worth, Texas, for the rollout of Germany’s first Lockheed Martin F-35A fighter jet, arguably the most significant weapon in the Bundeswehr’s modernization drive. Berlin has ordered 35 aircraft, with pilot training beginning next year in Arkansas and deliveries scheduled through 2029. Officials are already discussing a potential follow-on order of 15 more jets.
The F-35 is more than another procurement program. It secures Germany’s role in NATO nuclear sharing, unlocks new operational capabilities and ties the Luftwaffe into the alliance’s rapidly growing community of F-35 operators.
And it is only one example of reliance on U.S. arms-makers.
Advertisement
Germany’s rearmament increasingly runs through American production lines: CH-47F Chinook transport helicopters, P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, Patriot air-defense systems and key technologies for the future F127 air-defense frigate.
Hegseth praised Germany's higher defense spending and said it was a key step toward what he calls "NATO 3.0" — the idea that European allies will bear more of the burden of defending the continent while the U.S. pivots to other areas of the world.
“Europe must assume primary responsibility for its conventional defense,” he argued.
Transatlantic divide
But the views of Berlin and Washington are diverging.
Pistorius underlined that the major danger facing the continent is Russia, calling it “the greatest threat to the alliance, the West, and our way of life since the height of the Cold War.” He also cited challenges from Iran, North Korea and China.
The German minister stressed Berlin's continued support for Ukraine. The Trump administration has halted almost all new military aid to Kyiv since taking office.
Advertisement
Hegseth identified no specific threats and underlined that President Donald Trump's main mission was "American manufacturing, American made, American jobs."
For now, Germany's rearmament drive dovetails with that vision. Pistorius said: "Germany is investing and buying in the U.S., adding up to about $50 billion, creating growth and jobs in the United States of America."
But Germany is using its own resources and teaming up with other European countries on defense projects. Berlin is also increasingly frustrated that the U.S. is favoring its own needs — boosting production of Tomahawk missiles to rebuild its own stocks depleted by the war against Iran — which is delaying potential deliveries to Germany.
Berlin sees the Typhon launcher system and Tomahawk cruise missiles as essential for deterrence against Russia. The acquisition would give Germany something it has never possessed: the ability to strike targets deep behind enemy lines with conventional land-based precision weapons. The problem is that the capability Germany wants depends entirely on American production.
“I made it very clear that the timelines previously discussed are too slow from our perspective,” Pistorius said after raising the issue with Hegseth. The Americans, he added, had “taken note of this positively.”
Hegseth is leading a rethink of U.S. force posture in Europe, and the Trump administration has already pulled troops out of Germany. Asked after their meeting whether he had gained greater clarity about future U.S. deployments, Pistorius was blunt: “No, not yet.”
Advertisement
Pistorius insisted that buying more U.S. weapons would not undermine Germany's effort to boost its own capabilities.
Instead, Berlin wants German firms integrated into American supply chains, maintenance networks and licensed-production arrangements. Throughout the visit, Pistorius emphasized that German industry could help relieve production bottlenecks and expand capacity on both sides of the Atlantic.
"NATO needs to become more European in order to stay transatlantic," he said.

articles.title: ‘It Is a Pity’: China Could Stop the War but Leans Toward Russia, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday, Sept. 17, that China is not politically on Ukraine’s side in Russia’s war and instead leans toward Moscow, despite having enough influence to push Russian leader Vladimir Putin toward negotiations.
Zelensky made the remarks in an interview with Japanese public broadcaster NHK, excerpts from which he published on his official Telegram channel.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is a pity that China is not on our side in this war – politically. It is not even about weapons,” Zelensky said in the final excerpt.
He argued that China’s position was not neutral because Beijing appeared more open and willing to help Russia than Ukraine.
For a country as large and influential as China, being even “a little more” on Russia’s side has major consequences, Zelensky said.
China has leverage but has not used it
Zelensky said he had personally seen a North Korean-made missile in Ukraine but had not seen a Chinese missile used by Russia.
However, he said Chinese technology and equipment were reaching Russia, possibly together with specialists and technical expertise.
The Ukrainian president said he had never seen China publicly pressure Moscow to stop the war. He acknowledged that Beijing might be raising the issue privately during bilateral meetings but said there had been no visible result.
Zelensky pointed to Russia’s growing isolation from international energy and banking systems, Western sanctions and restrictions targeting its shadow fleet as areas in which China could exercise significant leverage.
6 Russian Aircraft Hit as Ukraine Strikes Deep Inside Russia
In his assessment, Beijing could find a way to push Putin toward negotiations but had chosen not to do so. He questioned whether refusing to act despite possessing such influence amounted to support for Moscow.
Zelensky said strong global leaders, including China’s leadership, could help stop the war quickly if they demonstrated sufficient political will.
Ukraine has repeatedly raised concerns about Chinese-origin technology found in Russian weapons. In July, Beijing had not visibly responded after Ukraine provided serial-number evidence linking Chinese-made components to Russian missiles and drones.
Kyiv Post also reported in August that Chinese components, including small turbojet engines, had helped Russia develop faster Shahed-type attack drones that are more difficult for Ukraine to intercept.
China says it strictly controls exports of dual-use goods and has opposed sanctions imposed on Chinese companies accused of helping Russia’s military industry.
Kyiv seeks Drone Deal with Japan
In another excerpt from the NHK interview, Zelensky called for deeper military-technology cooperation between Ukraine and Japan at both the government-to-government and business-to-business levels.
He noted that more than 70% of Ukraine’s defense industry is privately owned and said closer cooperation could increase bilateral trade, particularly in the defense sector.
Zelensky acknowledged differences between the two countries’ legal systems but argued that “when it comes to defense, there are no neutral countries.”
He identified maritime-surveillance, reconnaissance and demining drones, as well as air defense, cybersecurity and food security, as potential areas for cooperation.
Ukraine would like to conclude a Drone Deal with Japan, Zelensky said, adding that Ukrainian defense equipment could also prove useful to Tokyo.
Any decision to acquire it would, however, be up to Japan, he added.
North Korean training raises Pacific threat
Zelensky also warned that North Korea had sent between 30,000 and 50,000 soldiers to Russia, where they were able to obtain experience in real combat rather than through digital simulations.
In the second interview excerpt, he said the North Korean forces had suffered significant losses when they fought Ukrainian troops during the Kursk operation.
Afterward, Zelensky said, they avoided entering Ukrainian territory directly but continued training inside Russia, including alongside drone operators.
“They are training, working with drones and drone operators,” Zelensky said, describing the experience they were gaining as a major threat to security in the Pacific region.
Ukrainian military intelligence previously said that North Korea had deployed a new contingent of approximately 8,500 troops to Russia, including around 400 drone operators and 1,000 engineers and deminers.
Ukrainian intelligence estimated in August that around 25,000 North Korean personnel had served in Russia and that Moscow could seek tens of thousands more.
The growing partnership allows Russia to obtain additional troops, ammunition and missiles while giving Pyongyang practical experience in drone warfare, electronic warfare and modern high-intensity combat.

articles.title: Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
articles.body:
Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
KYIV, Sept 17 - Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people. It has also served as a proving ground for new weapons systems and raised an uncomfortable question for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization: Is the alliance prepared for the next war it might have to fight?
Five Ukrainian and Western defense officials told Reuters that developments on the battlefield are moving so quickly that some NATO weapons and tactics risk becoming outdated. While Ukraine – which is not an alliance member – adapts in weeks, NATO buys and develops systems over years, sometimes decades.
The Ukraine war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s haranguing of European allies have prompted many NATO members to dramatically increase their defense spending. The Pentagon is currently reviewing its military presence in European countries, which Trump has accused of sponging off U.S. protection and refusing to help prosecute his unpopular war against Iran.
Denys Shtilerman, the co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, a leading Ukrainian missile and drone builder, told Reuters that tanks are now “worthless” because a drone costing about $5,000 can destroy one. Yet Europe still spends heavily on tanks – which, say many military analysts, still have a key role to play in future battles.
Cheap drones have also transformed warfare in other ways. Troops gathering in groups or large vehicle convoys all become far easier targets.
“They are good at storming positions,” Oleksandr Pivnenko, Commander of the National Guard of Ukraine, said of the international troops his units trained with last year. “But if there’s a drone overhead and you don’t even look up, what do you think will happen to your squad?”
In June, Reuters attended a NATO military exercise near Paldiski in Estonia – a small Baltic country now fortifying its 210-mile border with Russia – in which American and European troops treated dozens of simulated casualties at wartime field hospitals. But the exercise took place with the assumption that NATO would command the airspace above the hospitals – no longer a given in the age of cheap, stealthy, long-distance drones.
Rather than simply receiving NATO training and assistance, Ukrainian officials described a growing role for Ukraine in teaching the alliance lessons drawn from the war with Russia. Yet they also said NATO’s military bureaucracy struggles to absorb those lessons. A Ukrainian officer who underwent NATO psychological operations training in Romania told Reuters that some alliance training materials still relied on case studies from World War Two. NATO didn’t respond to questions about the officials’ criticism of its training and bureaucracy.
The Ukraine war has also exposed a vulnerability that NATO officials say is far harder to solve: air and missile defense. Russia’s relentless barrages against Ukrainian cities have highlighted Europe's dependence on sophisticated U.S. anti-missile systems such as the Patriot, first used in the 1991 Gulf War. Ukraine has a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors – the missiles fired to destroy incoming threats.
Fearing that its reliance on Patriots might become a strategic vulnerability, Europe is building non-U.S. alternatives. Ukraine is awaiting delivery of the new French-Italian SAMP/T-NG air-defense system, designed to intercept ballistic missiles. France has promised to accelerate its deployment to Ukraine, and European diplomats previously told Reuters it was expected to arrive by next spring.
In a statement, the Ukrainian defense ministry said its soldiers and NATO’s had much to learn from each other, hailing Ukraine’s use of drones and radioelectronic warfare as “globally unmatched" and praising European efforts to help tackle Russia’s drone and missile bombardments.
In July, Ukraine and nine European allies launched an air-defense coalition that includes plans to jointly develop a new anti-ballistic missile system. Known as Freyja, the project is a consortium of about a dozen companies with Fire Point as the lead private-sector partner. The goal is to build a system that is cheaper and faster to produce than the Patriot, while ensuring that Europe, not the U.S., controls its manufacture.
“If you spend $20 billion on your air defense system, you must be independent in your security,” said Fire Point’s Shtilerman. REUTERS

articles.title: Autonomous AI threats leave US and China minutes to prevent nuclear crisis, experts warn
articles.body:
An AI system that interferes with a nuclear command network or launches a military cyber operation could leave Washington or Beijing with minutes to decide whether the other government attacked, according to US and Chinese security experts.
The experts, part of a US-China dialogue whose work helps inform official discussions, are urging both governments to prepare for such scenarios amid rising concerns about increasingly powerful and more autonomous systems.
Their proposals include red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyberattacks, and a hotline for incidents involving autonomous AI.
The recommendations were published last week ahead of planned government-level AI talks and an expected September 24 meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Authors Melanie Sisson, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution think tank, and Tianjiao Jiang, an associate professor at Fudan University, participated in the US-China AI and national security dialogue convened since 2019 by Brookings and Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy.
Red lines around nuclear systems
Their proposals show how the US-China AI rivalry is moving beyond competition over chips and advanced models into questions long associated with arms control: how to prevent accidents from being mistaken for attacks, limit machine-made military decisions and set communication protocols for nuclear-armed rivals when technology behaves unexpectedly.
China's State Security Minister Chen Yixin this week wrote in a government outlet that AI "fundamentally transforms the form of military struggle." He said it had moved from playing a supporting role on the battlefield to a key role, citing AI-directed strikes in the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Brookings Institution's Sisson argued that humans should retain sole authority to initiate AI-enabled cyberattacks against the other country's nuclear command, control and communications systems or strategically important infrastructure.
An autonomous system could malfunction, exceed its instructions, or be compromised, while the country under attack might struggle to tell whether the action was accidental or ordered by its rival.
Fudan University's Jiang proposed explicit red lines preventing AI from independently deciding to use nuclear weapons or autonomously attacking nuclear command systems, along with protections around critical infrastructure including energy, finance and healthcare.
He also urged a shared definition of "meaningful human control" to prevent both countries from using identical language to justify different levels of machine autonomy.
The idea builds on a principle endorsed by then-US president Joe Biden and Xi in November 2024 that humans should retain control over decisions to use nuclear weapons.
Lora Saalman, an associate senior fellow at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, wrote in February that this was an important point of US-China convergence even as both countries showed signs of integrating AI more deeply into nuclear and nuclear-related systems.
When machines move faster than humans
Jiang also proposed a dedicated US-China military hotline for AI incidents, warning that automated cyber exchanges could escalate too quickly for human intervention.
One country's defensive AI might automatically respond to suspicious activity, while the other side could interpret that response as an attack and retaliate before understanding what actually happened.
A hotline could allow one government to tell the other that an unusual AI operation was accidental, unauthorized or still under investigation before it was treated as deliberate state action.
However, experts including Carla Freeman at Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies have questioned the utility of the existing US-China military crisis communication hotline, citing Chinese officials' refusal to answer US counterparts' calls about the "spy balloon incident" in February 2023.
The Chinese bureaucracy's rigid top-down hierarchy also disempowers low-ranking officers from taking the initiative during engagements with US counterparts, she wrote in an article for War on the Rocks in January.
"No one in the Chinese system wants to communicate with the United States until the top leadership in consultation with relevant actors within China's party-state have decided on a response, which may take days if not longer," she said.
Views in Washington and Beijing
Neither government has publicly endorsed the Brookings-Tsinghua proposals, but China has increasingly placed AI inside its existing arms-control bureaucracy.
AI is a formal portfolio of the Foreign Ministry's Department of Arms Control, which also handles nuclear weapons, non-proliferation, missiles and other international security issues.
Shen Jian, China's ambassador for disarmament affairs, told a UN meeting in Geneva in June that military AI could affect strategic stability and raise risks of miscalculation and conflict escalation, and that weapons should remain under human control. China also argues that AI safety should not become a pretext for technological barriers.
Washington has no equivalent single arms-control home for AI, with national security policy spread across the White House National Security Council, State Department, Pentagon and other agencies.
Both governments remain wary of measures that could slow their own technological development. Trump has warned broad restraints could hand China an advantage, while Beijing views many US technology controls as attempts to preserve American dominance.

articles.title: North Korea accused of using overseas workers finance nuclear weapons
articles.body:
A report has found that North Korean overseas workers raised between $US450 million ($633 million) and $US800 million last year for the authoritarian state's nuclear weapons program.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team report — co-signed by a range of Western governments and US allies — details "systemic evasion of UN sanctions by the DPRK [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] and other countries through a global network of unlawful overseas labour".
It says the overseas labourers were working primarily in China and Russia and numbered anywhere between 35,000 and 101,000 workers.
A host of Western governments and US allies say North Korea's network of illegal labourers in Russia and China raised between $US450 million ($633 million) and $US800 million last year for Kim Jong Un's nuclear weapons program, helping Pyongyang evade United Nations sanctions.
Human rights groups have long decried North Korea's forced labour program, saying thousands of workers are subjected to control, abuse and coercion as they earn hard cash for the regime.
In 2024 a coalition of developed countries set up the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) to monitor North Korea's efforts to dodge sanctions after Russia used its Security Council veto to dismantle a UN panel of experts tracking the issue.
This morning that same coalition — which draws in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, the US and the UK — issued a report detailing the "systemic evasion of UN sanctions by the DPRK [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] and other countries through a global network of unlawful overseas labour".
The report says that North Korea maintains an army of between 35,000 and 101,000 labourers overseas.
While at least 17 countries are "suspected of continuing to host labourers" from North Korea the vast majority are working in Russia and China.
China has always denied hosting illegal workers from North Korea — and pushed out at least 10,000 workers between 2023 and 2025 — but human rights groups and investigative reporters have documented how thousands can still be found working in Chinese factories, plants and fishing fleets.
The MSMT report estimates that China still hosts between 20,000 and 70,000 North Korean labourers.
North Korea is also sending increasing numbers of labourers to Russia, which the report says has created a student visa scheme to "camouflage" North Korean labourers.
Moscow and Pyongyang have formed an increasingly tight military and strategic partnership in the last three years, with North Korea emerging as one of Russia's key backers in its invasion of Ukraine.
The MSMT report estimates there are between 15,000 and 30,000 working in Russia "as of the end of 2025", with North Korean labourers manufacturing military drones on Russian soil to bolster Vladimir Putin's war effort.
"Overseas North Korean labourers face low wages, work 12 to 18 hours per day, six or seven days per week, and are required to forfeit 80-90 per cent of their income — or more — to the DPRK government," the report says.
"Labourers are also charged an additional fee of up to 30 per cent of the funds they send as remittances to family, in addition to paying other fees, including those related to travel, food, and lodging.
"Often, this amounts up to complete wage confiscation."
Lara Strangways from the international human rights foundation Global Rights Compliance called the report "alarming" and said it validated the work done by several watchdog groups.
"North Korean workers are being channelled through Russian labour brokers into a system built on debt bondage, confiscated documents and constant surveillance, generating hard currency for Pyongyang," she said.
"This is a problem which must be urgently confronted as the scale and breadth of state-sponsored forced labour expands due to the DPRK's intensifying need for foreign currency.
"The labour brokers facilitating these arrangements, and the companies profiting from this exploitation, must be identified and sanctioned."
The governments behind the joint report have not committed to any new sanctions on Russian or Chinese companies, but said in their joint statement they were "sharing this information with the international community to highlight the significant risks associated with employing North Korean overseas labourers and the need to deter the employment of such labourers".
"We encourage all UN member states to raise awareness and hold responsible parties and facilitators accountable for UNSCR [UN Security Council Resolution] violations, including through domestic action," they said.

articles.title: Ukraine live: Explosions shake Kyiv as US Congress advances new sanctions on Moscow
articles.body:
Russia struck a Tanzanian-flagged civilian ship in the Black Sea, killing its captain, Ukraine said Thursday, after loud explosions were heard across Kyiv overnight. Authorities have issued a missile alert in the capital, an AFP journalist reported. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Russian missile and drone attacks injure at least 19, including children, in Ukraine
A Russian barrage of missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital and the surrounding region injured at least 19 people overnight and into Thursday morning, authorities said.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said the overnight attacks struck more than 10 locations in the city, while 33 sites were damaged in the wider region. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, the administration said in a statement on Telegram.
Armenia leader says would not oppose Russian base pullout
Yerevan will not object if Russia closes its military base in the country, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has said, adding that the base is no longer vital to national security.
The base, near Armenia's border with Turkey, has been a key symbol of Moscow's military influence in the South Caucasus.
Pashinyan's comments come as Armenia pursues an increasingly pro-Western foreign policy and distances itself from traditional ally Moscow's orbit.
Ukraine receives 252 bodies in swap with Russia
Ukraine has received the bodies of 252 people in an exchange of war dead with Russia, Ukrainian authorities said Thursday.
Russia received 23 bodies in return, Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliev was quoted as saying by the RBK news outlet.
The exchange of prisoners of war and fallen soldiers is one of the few areas of cooperation between the warring sides.
"As a result of repatriation measures, the bodies of 252 deceased persons have been returned to Ukraine," Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said.
Police and other officials will "conduct all necessary examinations and identify the repatriated bodies", it added.
Poland says no violation of its airspace during Russian strikes on Ukraine
The Polish army says that no violation of Polish airspace was recorded and that military aircraft have finished their operations.
Airports in Rzeszow and Lublin reopened after their temporary closure.
Turkey proposes a deal between Ukraine and Russia to end Black Sea shipping attacks
Turkey has sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine that would end attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, a Turkish diplomat told AFP on Thursday.
"We have shared a text of a memorandum, a draft text, with the Russians and the Ukrainians to come up with a solution to those strikes taking place in the Black Sea," the diplomat said.
No damage to border crossing points after a Russian drone attack in western Ukraine, Ukraine's border service says
Explosions sounded several kilometres from the Ukraine-Polish border during a Russian drone attack, Ukrainian official says
Ukraine says explosions sounded several kilometres from Polish border
Explosions were heard several kilometres from Ukraine's border with Poland during a Russian drone attack, a Ukrainian official has said.
Ukraine's border service said there were no reports of damage to border crossings.
Russia and Ukraine exchange fallen soldiers' bodies, BELTA reports
Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of their war dead on Thursday with Moscow handing over
252 corpses and receiving 23 bodies in the swap at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border, Belarusian state news agency BELTA reported.
Poland scrambles military aircraft due to Russian strikes on Ukraine
Poland has scrambled military aircraft due to Russian drone strikes on Ukraine, the army has said.
"These measures are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting airspace, particularly in areas adjacent to the threatened regions," the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said on X.
US sanctions complicate Ukraine peace efforts, says Kremlin
The United States imposing fresh sanctions on Russia will complicate efforts to broker peace with Ukraine, the Kremlin has said, a day after the US Congress approved legislation to pressure Moscow over its war.
"Of course, the imposition of any further sanctions by the US will definitely complicate the search for, and efforts towards, a peaceful resolution in Ukraine," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
France's Macron convenes political parties to discuss Ukraine and Mideast
French President Emmanuel has convened the chiefs of the different political parties represented in parliament to a meeting on Friday morning to discuss the crises in the Middle East and Ukraine and their consequences on the energy market.
The meeting will be held at 10:30am local time (0830 GMT) and military and intelligence officers will share the information they have provided to Macron, his office said in a statement.
Ukraine plans record defence spending in 2027
The Ukrainian government plans to spend a record two thirds of its budget on defence next year as costs mount in its war with Russia, government documents showed.
Russia's four-and-a-half-year offensive has battered Ukraine's economy, causing billions of dollars in destruction and punching a huge hole in its neighbour's finances.
The war-torn country initially used its own revenues to pay for defence spending but has increasingly relied on foreign backers for these outlays.
The Ukrainian government will seek an additional $53 billion in foreign aid next year, including from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, it said.
Russian drone attack on Tanzania-flagged vessel kills one, says Ukraine
A Russian drone attack on Tanzania-flagged vessel en route to a Ukrainian port killed the vessel's captain and injured three crew, Ukraine's infrastructure ministry has said.
Information regarding the vessel's condition was being clarified, the ministry said in a statement on Telegram.
Ukraine's Zelensky claims strike on Russian oil refinery
Ukraine has claimed the strike on the Yaroslavl oil refinery that was reported earlier by Russian officials.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also reported a strike on a military airfield in Rostov, which damaged military aircrafts and helicopters.
"There have also been good results in the Black Sea," he said on X, without giving further detail.
Ukraine's Zelensky appoints acting prosecutor general
President Volodymyr Zelensky has appointed Anton Kovalskyi as Ukraine's acting prosecutor general, a presidential decree has shown.
Zelensky removed former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko by decree earlier this week, with lawmakers approving the decision in a vote on Tuesday.
Kovalskyi, 42, has since July 2025 headed the regional prosecutor's office in the Khmelnytskyi region.
Russian attack on Kyiv injures at least 16
A Russian barrage of missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital has injured at least 16 people overnight and into the morning, local authorities said.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attacks were recorded at more than 10 locations. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, it said in a statement on Telegram.
Ukraine’s Air Force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets in the overnight attack. The main areas targeted were Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
Russia's parliamentary vote features no real opposition to Putin
Starting Friday and lasting through Sunday, Russians will elect members of the country's lower house of parliament, the State Duma.
The elections feature the Kremlin's main party, United Russia, and nine others that all support President Vladimir Putin’s policies. The only party that dared to oppose the war in Ukraine has been barred from the ballot.
The Kremlin wants the polls — the first since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022 — to underline public support for the war and give a veneer of legitimacy to its action.
Drone attack damages oil refinery in Russia's Yaroslavl, governor says
A Ukrainian drone attack overnight damaged an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, northeast of Moscow, regional Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said in a post on Telegram.
The governor later said the fire had been put out.
Donald Trump strengthened NATO by pushing allies to increase their defence spending, Finland's president said, describing a "pragmatic" relationship with a US leader who is "a man of his own mind".
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Tuesday dismissed questions about a Russian oligarch who paid for a party at Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding earlier this year and said President Donald Trump did not know the Russian.
The European Union must ramp up measures against the Kremlin, including reviewing the issuance of tourist visas to Russians, to counter Moscow's "hybrid attacks", foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

articles.title: A crisis on two fronts: Saudi Arabia's mounting security dilemma
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
A crisis on two fronts: Saudi Arabia's mounting security dilemma
A drone attack launched from Iraqi territory last week against Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline to the Red Sea has revived the prospect of a two-front confrontation for Riyadh.
As the situation in Yemen spirals further out of anyone’s control, Saudi Arabia’s options for managing both fronts are narrowing.
The Houthis have completed their takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing Mocha and the islands of Perim, Zuqar, and Hanish, which command the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
While the Yemeni government’s counteroffensive has since shifted toward Marib and Jawf, the front lines remain fluid.
A second front opens
On Thursday, several drones struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline south of Medina, causing injuries and damage and forcing Riyadh to shut the pipeline as a precaution.
The Saudi foreign ministry said the drones had been launched from Iraq and would not retaliate “at this stage,” at the request of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
Baghdad dismissed the commander who led operations in Missan province after an investigation traced the drones to launch platforms near al-Shib, on the Iranian border, and closed three crossings, Shalamsheh, al-Shib and al-Mandali, to stop the attackers fleeing into Iran.
Al-Zaidi has accepted an Iranian request for a joint investigation. No group has claimed the strike, and an alliance of Iran-backed factions has denied hitting the pipeline.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq called it “an honour that we do not claim”. Shalamsheh and al-Shib reopened to passenger traffic on Sunday, though not yet to trade, with a full reopening due by Thursday.
It is not the first time Riyadh has traced an attack on its oil infrastructure to Iraq. On 29 July, US and Saudi forces struck Iran-aligned Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) factions accused of hitting Saudi facilities in the Eastern Province. Twenty PMF fighters and five Iranian advisers were reportedly killed. Riyadh called it self-defence.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq initially threatened retaliation over the July strikes before backing down under pressure from Iraqi figures, including Hadi al-Amiri. Diplomatic efforts through August did not stop last Thursday’s attack.
The Shia Coordination Framework in Baghdad remains divided over how to disarm Iran-backed factions ahead of a 30 September deadline. Part of the problem is that some factions are deeply embedded in Iraq’s security apparatus and maintain close ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
That disarmament push may not even solve the underlying problem. Tamer Badawi, an Iraq analyst and associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that the Islamic Resistance in Iraq’s denial, if it “proves accurate,” could mean Iran’s Quds Force “may be conducting attacks via new groupings”.
Even if known factions like Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada disarm, “other new and unknown groups can launch transborder attacks from Iraqi territories”.
Baghdad, Badawi added, lacks “consistent control over the Iran-aligned groups” and the “ground-to-air capabilities” needed to stop such strikes.
“It’s most certainly the case that there is coordination between Tehran, armed networks in Iraq, and Ansarallah,” he told The New Arab, though it is “taking much less of a public and celebrated appearance” than when Iraqi factions and Ansarullah synchronised attacks against Israel after 7 October.
The Institute for the Study of War described the strike as part of “a coordinated effort with other Axis of Resistance members to coerce Saudi Arabia to meet Houthi demands by attacking Saudi energy infrastructure”.
The same assessment linked the attack to the Houthi campaign around Bab al-Mandeb, saying the Houthis are “setting conditions to establish” the strait “as an Axis of Resistance-controlled body of water,” which it called “unacceptable for US national security and economic interests”.
Saudi strategy under pressure
The latest Houthi offensive began on 3 September across Taiz and Hodeidah, producing Yemen’s biggest territorial changes since a 2022 truce halted the civil war. It also undoes years of Saudi effort to reduce exposure.
Riyadh led a coalition against the Houthis from 2015, scaled back after a costly air campaign, and pursued a peace roadmap from 2023.
Direct hostilities resumed in July, after Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport and the Houthis blockaded Red Sea ports. Last Tuesday, Houthi missiles and drones hit four southern Saudi cities, injuring at least 73 people. Riyadh has relied on tens of thousands of Yemeni troops rather than deploy its own.
The Houthis claimed a fresh strike of their own on Sunday, saying they hit weapons depots and command centres at the Sharurah military base in southern Saudi Arabia. An Iranian commercial vessel was struck the same day in the Strait of Hormuz, a reminder that Riyadh’s other maritime exit remains unsettled too.
Those forces have struggled for familiar reasons. Coordination between units has been patchy, reinforcement mechanisms weak, and Saudi air support limited. Someone still has to fight on the ground, and the units expected to do that are the ones already exposed as weakest.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG), said the Houthis’ hold on Bab al-Mandeb has already changed their leverage.
“It’s clear that the Houthis now have a greater influence over the Bab al-Mandab,” he told The New Arab. “It also gives them room to expand toward the other side of Yemen and further weaken the government forces that Saudi Arabia is supporting.”
Nagi said Riyadh has few good options left. “I don’t think the Saudis have many good options to contain the situation now,” he said.
“Things have basically gone from bad to worse. If they want to contain it, they’ll probably have to make some concessions, because the Houthis are now negotiating from a much stronger position.”
That bind predates last week’s advance. Reversing the Houthi gains risks pulling Saudi Arabia back into the ground war it spent a decade trying to leave. Leaving them unanswered risks losing the coastline and the pipeline’s approach to Yanbu for good.
Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the risk advisory firm Basha Report, said that “the situation on Yemen’s West Coast remains fluid”.
The coalition, he told The New Arab, “appears to have resumed limited airstrikes against Houthi positions,” while the Southern Giants Brigades and National Shield Forces “have stabilised a new defensive line south of the strait,” with units withdrawn from the coast regrouping elsewhere.
Houthi casualties from the offensive that ended 9 September are “heavy,” though unconfirmed.
Washington stops short
The Houthi advance has already pushed Riyadh to seek military help it said only two months ago it did not need. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called President Donald Trump twice on Thursday as Saudi-backed forces retreated, asking in the second call for the US to authorise strikes against the Houthis. Trump declined.
Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM chief, travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday, and around 200 US personnel are now in the kingdom, with more than 100 focused on intelligence and targeting, according to reports.
In practice, Riyadh is managing the war largely alone, with indirect support, limited airstrikes, stronger air defences, and a parallel push for Oman-mediated talks.
That mix of escalation and diplomacy is not necessarily a contradiction. It reflects a Saudi calculation that military pressure and a negotiated off-ramp serve the same goal, keeping the Houthis from consolidating gains without a return to the costly ground war Riyadh spent years trying to exit.
Saudi oil route comes under pressure
The pipeline gives Saudi Arabia only a partial way around Hormuz. It lets crude bypass the strait and reach Yanbu, but tankers carrying those exports south still have to cross the Red Sea toward Bab al-Mandeb. Bypass capacity, in practice, is not secure supply.
Markets are already registering some of that risk. Saudi Arabia’s benchmark stock index fell 1.3% on Sunday, and Aramco shares 1.6%, as investors weighed the pipeline’s precautionary shutdown. Reuters put the exposure at roughly 4% of global oil supply.
The Houthis say their blockade targets only Saudi vessels. Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels a day in August to 6 million bpd, its lowest level in three decades, according to the International Energy Agency, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab al-Mandeb.
Nagi sees a deliberate logic behind the timing. Iran, he argued, has a clear interest in pressuring Saudi Arabia while Hormuz is already disrupted, and in hitting Saudi energy exports via the Yanbu reroute now within Houthi reach.
It also challenges the regional order Washington has been building ahead of the midterms.
“That obviously benefits Iran at this moment,” he said, “because it gives Tehran another way to put pressure on its regional adversaries and the global economy.”
Regional test
The escalation is also testing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement Saudi Arabia signed with Pakistan and Turkey in August, committing each to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Whether it extends to an Iraq-origin attack is untested.
The East-West Pipeline was built to solve one problem, Saudi Arabia’s exposure at Hormuz. It is now exposed from both directions. Drones from Iraq can hit the infrastructure carrying crude to Yanbu, while Houthi forces at Bab al-Mandeb can threaten the ships carrying it onward.
That vulnerability-reduction strategy has instead multiplied where Riyadh can be tested.
But the coordination of strikes looks strategic more than operational. Tehran does not need to order a specific attack for it to serve the same purpose as the Houthi campaign at Bab al-Mandeb.
Confirmation of an operational link between the two fronts would turn this from two crises into one campaign against the infrastructure Saudi Arabia built to feel safe from either.
For now, Riyadh is reinforcing Yemeni forces, working with Baghdad to trace last week’s drone attackers, and leaning on Oman’s channel with the Houthis.
It is, for the moment, a strategy of management rather than resolution.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors
Follow him on X: @frencio_schiavi

articles.title: The US House just passed the first major Russia oil sanctions in two years—one signature stands between them and law
articles.body:
The US House of Representatives has approved sweeping new sanctions on Russia and the countries and companies that help finance its war, sending the measure to the president to sign into law, The Hill reported. The vote breaks a nearly two-year stretch in which Congress passed no major measure to back Ukraine. It also hands Washington fresh power to choke the oil money that keeps Moscow's war running.
For most of the full-scale war, US backing for Kyiv came through emergency spending battles, not laws built to cut off Moscow's income. Washington's long wager that negotiations would end the fighting kept its sharpest economic tools on the shelf. That bet has now shifted toward squeezing the customers who keep the Kremlin's oil trade alive.
The vote and what comes next
In the House, 58 Democrats broke from their party's leaders on 16 September to join most Republicans. The bill passed 262-159, with 203 Republicans and one independent also voting yes, and seven Republicans joining 152 Democrats against.
Whether the full weight of the bill lands is now Trump's call. A White House official said he planned to sign it, and the White House had pushed House Republican leaders to move it. The bill directs him to impose the tariffs and mandates sanctions on Putin, senior officials, and Russian banks, though he can waive them by certifying that it serves US national interests, and how far he goes stays uncertain.
His posture on Russia keeps shifting. Days before the vote, he urged Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries. He said the strikes were pushing diesel prices up worldwide. Those same strikes drain the war economy this bill sets out to squeeze.
What the sanctions do
The bill directs Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five biggest buyers of Russian crude, the five biggest buyers of its gas, and the five countries doing most to help Moscow evade oil sanctions—a target aimed squarely at China and India. Countries whose Russian gas imports are less than 15% of everything Russia exports in gas, and that take significant steps to cut them, would be exempt from the gas-based tariff. There is no such carve-out for crude.
It also blacklists Russian officials, banks, and the aging tankers of Russia's shadow fleet, the vessels that move sanctioned crude around Western restrictions. The measure also extends US sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors, a piece Trump asked for. That is why the bill's full name is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
US sanctions 13 Iran-Belarus-China entities supplying Iran’s IRGC. That’s three of four “Axis of Upheaval” states
Why a stalled bill finally moved
For more than a year, the package sat frozen. It had a veto-proof majority of co-sponsors, but the White House wanted room to negotiate with Moscow, and the bill never reached a vote. Its author, Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, spent more than a year negotiating the measure before he died in July. Lawmakers in both parties revived and fast-tracked it in his name, and Trump dropped his resistance and signaled he would sign.
Not everyone wanted it. Most House Democrats voted against, saying the bill hands the president broad new tariff powers and lets him waive away the sanctions it claims to impose. Nearly a dozen Republicans privately pressed leaders to strip the new powers out, alarmed they could push up prices at home before the midterm elections. Their leaders moved it through anyway. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had lobbied for weeks, even watching an early Senate vote from the chamber.
"To Vladimir Putin—we have your number," said Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-wrote the bill, after the vote. "And to Ukraine—you are not alone."
Kyiv's response
Ukraine welcomed the vote within hours. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked the House for its bipartisan leadership and said Ukraine honors Graham's legacy. Parliament speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk thanked both chambers of Congress and House Speaker Mike Johnson. He singled out Blumenthal for carrying the bill through after Graham's death. What matters for Ukraine, Stefanchuk said, is that pressure on Russia's war funding is turning into concrete decisions.
President Zelenskyy called the timing symbolic: the House voted during another Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. The bill and other strong sanctions steps are "an extremely powerful instrument capable of stopping this terrorist war," he said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: North Korean missiles seen in Ukraine, no Chinese ones, but Beijing exerts no pressure on Russia to end war
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky believes that China could exert pressure on the Russian leadership to end the war, but refrains from doing so for its own reasons, he stated in an interview with Japan's public broadcaster NHK.
"I have seen a real North Korean-made missile in Ukraine. I have not seen Chinese missiles. But I know that their technologies find their way to Russia. The equipment they use comes from China, presumably along with specialists and technologies. I do not see China pressing Russia to end the war. I have never seen this. Perhaps they do it during some of their bilateral meetings, I do not know," Zelensky said.
He noted that China wields enormous influence over Russia, especially now amid extensive sanctions, the shadow fleet, and severed energy and banking systems. He expressed confidence that Beijing could find a way to push Vladimir Putin toward negotiations, adding that its failure to act amounts to support.
Zelensky called it regrettable that China is political on the side of Russia, clarifying that it is not about weapons, but political will. He stated that the war could be stopped instantly by strong leaders, including China, and expressed disappointment that Beijing is not on Ukraine's side, describing its stance as leaning closer to Russia through openness and readiness to help.
Regarding North Korea, the president reported that Pyongyang has deployed between 30,000 and 50,000 soldiers to Russia, while Moscow has provided them with real combat experience and training. He added that North Korean troops are learning, working with drones, and training, which poses a major security concern, particularly for the Pacific region.
Addressing bilateral ties, Zelensky emphasized that Ukraine is eager to build military-technology cooperation with Japan, noting that there are no neutral countries when it comes to defense. He suggested potential cooperation in marine monitoring, reconnaissance, demining, air defense, cybersecurity, and food security, and mentioned that Ukraine had sought to establish a Drone Deal with Japan.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Drone kills Russian commander just decorated after fake victory claim
articles.body:
- 
  Ukrainian drone forces have killed a Russian general who had just been made a Hero of Russia after false claims that Moscow’s forces had captured the Donetsk city of Kostiantynivka. Maj Gen Anton Grunis died in eastern Ukraine on Saturday. “General Grunis was eliminated on September 12,” said Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi, adding that the general was the seventh Russian military commander killed by his drone forces. Another Russian commander, Apti Alaudinov, posted confirmation that Grunis had died.
- 
  The battle for Kostiantynivka is gruelling for Ukraine but war analysts say it remains contested. Grunis reported personally to Vladimir Putin earlier this year that his troops helped capture Kostiantynivka and was praised by the Russian president for “doing the work”. The territorial claim remains heavily disputed – the US-based Institute for the Study of War said Russian forces had infiltrated but not fully seized the city, and Russia’s claim was part of a wider information campaign to “portray the Ukrainian frontlines as collapsing”. Grunis received the Gold Star Hero of Russia award at a ceremony in late August.
- 
  Russian airstrikes damaged buildings in Kyiv and injured three in the Black Sea port city of Odesa in the early hours of Thursday, officials said. In Kyiv, debris fell on warehouses and near a petrol station, among other locations, said the mayor, Vitali Klitschko. Three people, including a child, were injured as Russia hit a 19-storey apartment building in Odesa, authorities said.
- 
  Russian drones struck a passenger bus, killing five people, as well as attacking a train in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, Ukrainian officials said. “There is no military logic to this, just another act of brutality,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The bus was hit near the frontline city of Nikopol. Seven more people were wounded, said the Dnipropetrovsk region’s governor. Russian drones attacked a passenger train three times in Ukraine’s southern Mykolaiv region, the acting regional governor said. Passengers and crew were evacuated and no one was hurt. Zelenskyy said that in addition, a locomotive was struck in Kovel near the border with Poland.
- 
  Russian shelling on Wednesday killed one person in the southern Kherson region, and in the port of Odesa one death was reported. Russian attacks injured more than a dozen people in Sumy in the north and Kropyvnytskyi in central Ukraine. The Russia-installed head of areas of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region held by Moscow said a Ukrainian drone strike killed one person. Officials in Russia’s border Belgorod region said six people were injured in Ukrainian attacks.
- 
  The Russian Gerbera-2 drone found in the Baltic Sea off Poland was armed with explosives, officials said on Wednesday. Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Monday that the military had located the drone near the village of Rusinowo in north-western Poland and recovered it from the sea. The drone was thought to have been lost by Russia during test manoeuvres over the Baltic. Polish military prosecutors are investigating whether legal proceedings can be launched, presumably against Russia, for “causing an incident that endangers the life or health of many people and property of great value”.
- 
  The Russian government has extended a ban on diesel exports until the end of October. The ban had been due to end this month. Russia introduced restrictions on exports of gasoline, jet fuel and diesel because of domestic fuel shortages driven by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries. Reuters reported that fuel market data indicates three of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries were forced to significantly cut output or halt production altogether in September because of damage caused by drone attacks. Russia’s Rosneft-owned oil refineries in the Volga river cities of Syzran and Saratov have stopped processing after Ukrainian drone attacks this month, Reuters reported on Wednesday citing three industry sources.
- 
  Britain’s defence ministry has named a 40-year-old intelligence officer who died in a road crash away from the frontlines in Ukraine on Saturday. Maj Paul Wilks was commissioned from Sandhurst in 2012 and joined the Intelligence Corps, where he remained throughout his career. His commanding officer described Wilks as a “man of great intellect”, who often spoke of his love for his wife and two sons.
- 
  The chief of defence intelligence described Wilks as “one of the most talented intelligence officers of his generation”. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Wilks “served this country with pride and dedication”. A small number of British personnel serve in Ukraine providing security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces. Britain’s MoD previously announced paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December as he watched Ukrainian forces testing a new defensive capability.
- 
  A Russian strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv that stored props for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s former TV studio, the company said on Wednesday, adding that its staff were unharmed. Zelenskyy co-founded the Kvartal 95 production company in 2003 while working as a comedian. “We lost a large number of sets, costumes, and items that for 20 years had been part of our concerts, TV shows, movies, and series,” Kvartal 95 said. Zelenskyy spent much of his early career working in television, including in Russia. In 2013, he co-presented Russian state TV’s New Year’s Eve show. Kvartal 95 ceased work in Russia following Moscow’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1666: Ukraine’s counteroffensive disrupts Russia’s Donetsk encirclement plan
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant supplying missiles Moscow uses to bomb Ukrainian cities. ATESH says its agent disabled the power supply at the Voronezh facility, disrupting production of components used in Russian weapons.
Ukraine's Vivaldi counteroffensive disrupts Russia's plan to encircle Donetsk Fortress Belt – ISW. Ukrainian forces have likely advanced beyond the territory publicly disclosed by Kyiv, while Russian sources increasingly acknowledge setbacks around Lyman.
Russian general killed in Ukraine weeks after telling Putin Kostiantynivka was captured. Major General Anton Grunis was killed in occupied Donetsk Oblast after leading Russian forces on the Kostiantynivka front.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine put an Italian-Swiss Skyguard into combat duty. The missile inside is a Cold War design derived from the American Sparrow. Spain and Italy delivered Skyguard/Aspide starting in 2022. The 38th Regiment just showed it on combat duty for the first time.
Ukrainian border unit's HIMERA B1 relay took 10 strikes from Russia's FPV drones and guided bombs. Last one leveled building and tower, and relay kept working. Border guards dug the HIMERA B1 out of the rubble because it was still transmitting.
Russia ships armor to Libya despite mounting vehicle losses in Ukraine. Two sanctioned cargo vessels crossed the Mediterranean without broadcasting location data. Russian and Libyan authorities have not disclosed who was to receive their cargo.
Ukraine's Build with Ukraine has 200-plus foreign cooperation bids pending decision. Its arms industry, representing 400-plus firms, wants to help fix mechanism. The Council of Defence Industry wants a costly new export-permit fee scrapped.
In April, 24 Ukrainian companies ran their own air defense. By mid-September, 81 do — about one new firm per day. They've already downed 20-plus Russian drones.
International
A drone came down beside a Bundeswehr air base, weeks after Berlin blamed Moscow for the Leipzig airport attack. The drone's owner and origin are still unknown, and investigators are collecting further parts before saying anything about how it came down.
For first time, foreign government is funding Ukrainian drone school: Canada picks foundation that has already bought Ukraine nearly $50M in drones. Canada, once behind on drones, gets Ukraine's combat experience in return.
Humanitarian and social impact
Strikes on UN warehouses push aid money from delivery to protection. The UN is weighing underground storage for Ukraine aid supplies after Russia hit 10 of its facilities this year.
Russian drone killed five people on a scheduled minibus in southeastern Ukraine. The vehicle was running an intercity route through a district that sits across the river from Russian-held ground when the strike caught it.
Political and legal developments
US charges five as alleged Kremlin assassination network reaches American soil. Prosecutors say the network expanded from targeting Russian dissidents and defectors to arranging attacks against European countries supporting Ukraine.
He thought Ukrainian army uniform would hide what he did under occupation. It didn't. Man who guarded Kherson's Russian-run prison drew eight years. He guarded cells holding captured Ukrainian resistance members, then hid inside the army before the SBU caught him at a training center.
Kushner's "win-win" peace deal is impossible when Putin wants all of Ukraine — Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian president said he knew Putin would never change his goal, and that the deal formula was built on a misreading of what Russia wanted.

articles.title: Leaked photos and munition depletion expose devastating toll of Iranian strikes on US bases
articles.body:
Leaked photos and munition depletion expose devastating toll of Iranian strikes on US bases
TEHRAN – A mounting body of leaked evidence and admissions from within the American defense establishment has shattered the Pentagon’s carefully curated narrative of invulnerability, revealing unprecedented devastation across US military installations in West Asia resulting from precision Iranian missile and drone strikes.
Photographic evidence obtained by CBS News and leaked directly by active-duty American personnel—deliberately bypassing rigid military censorship—provides the first conclusive visual documentation of flattened hangars, obliterated command infrastructure, and hollowed-out barracks across several regional bases.
At Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, photographic evidence confirms a catastrophic direct hit on a Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control (AWACS) aircraft, its tail severed and its radar-carrying fuselage gutted by flames. Similar scenes of ruin were documented at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a primary desert staging hub for US ground forces and armored units. The imagery starkly illustrates that conventional US blast fortifications, such as concrete “T-walls,” have proven utterly useless against the kinetic force of modern Iranian aerial operations.
The visual disclosures substantiate a damning report released by the US Department of War Inspector General, which disclosed military equipment losses amounting to $3.7 billion—including the destruction or heavy damage of nearly 60 aircraft. In its mandatory briefing to Congress, the watchdog confirmed that US Central Command (CENTCOM) sustained direct strikes across eight countries: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan.
The disclosures have laid bare severe morale degradation and disillusionment within American ranks. Rebutting US War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s previous dismissal of Iranian projectiles as mere “squirters” breaching base perimeters, one deployed soldier admitted: “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public. We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face… We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.”
Compounding Washington’s operational crisis is the unsustainable attrition of its high-end air defense umbrella. According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, American forces burned through an unprecedented volume of critical munitions during a recent Iranian salvo targeting Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. US batteries fired between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptors alongside more than a dozen THAAD systems to counter an attack of approximately 20 ballistic missiles—an expenditure equivalent to an entire week’s inventory in earlier phases of the conflict.
Despite launching over 70 multi-million-dollar interceptors, the layered defense failed to avert catastrophic failure. Iranian missiles equipped with warheads that separate into multiple sub-munitions penetrated the defensive net, scoring direct hits on US fighter jets and support aircraft stationed on the Jordanian tarmac.
Experts note that the air-defense math has decisively turned against Washington. While Pentagon officials publicly insist stockpiles remain adequate, the Inspector General’s report conceded that the conflict has induced “strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.” With manufacturer Lockheed Martin producing only 620 Patriot interceptors in 2025 against an annual target of 2,000, US interceptor stockpiles are being depleted at a rate Washington cannot sustain.
As Iran’s missile forces continue to demonstrate operational adaptation—employing maneuverable warheads, varied trajectories, and precise targeting—the combination of scorched hangars on the ground and dwindling stockpiles in US arsenals confirms that the era of Western military deterrence in the region has reached an irreversible tipping point.

articles.title: Ukraine kept this strike drone secret for two years—its maker says it has destroyed more than 350 Russian systems
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone maker has revealed it built a strike weapon it kept classified, deputy director Andrii Rymaruk told Radio NV. For two years, Ukrspecsystems, known for manufacturing Ukraine's SHARK reconnaissance drones, hid its connection to the RAM-2X strike drone, even as crews used it to hunt Russia's costly air defenses and missile launchers deep behind the front. By 2025, it had quietly become the Defense Forces' flagship mid-strike drone.
Ukraine's war on Russia's air defenses increasingly runs on drones its own industry builds and fields in secret, revealed only once they have already destroyed the enemy's costliest launchers and radars. Holding one back that long lets its crews rack up strikes before Moscow can study the weapon and build a counter—and this maker went public only once wrecked drones had reached Russian hands.
Why come out now
The RAM-2X first flew in combat in early 2024, but the maker kept its role secret. Rymaruk said the company wanted the drone and its crews to finish the job first—destroy what needed destroying—before talking. Once shot-down units reached the enemy and turned up on social media, silence no longer protected anything. So after two years, Ukrspecsystems unveiled the drone at the MSPO defense expo in Kielce, Poland.
What it kills
This is a mid-strike drone—a loitering munition that flies deep behind the lines, circles, and dives into its target. Its victims include S-400 and S-300 air defenses, the systems Russia uses to shoot down aircraft, and Iskander launchers that fire ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities.
Rymaruk put the RAM-2X's own tally at more than 350 Russian systems destroyed since 2024, while Defender Media, which interviewed him, reported more than 1,000 targets over two years. Ukrspecsystems credits the wider RAM series, which reaches back to a fixed-wing model supplied from late 2022, with more than 450 target engagements, over 400 of them against air defenses. Today, it destroys 50 to 60 pieces of Russian equipment a month.
How far, how many
The drone has grown fast. It flew 140 km in 2024 and now hits targets up to 180 km, almost 230 km in good conditions, and a crew from the 429th Achilles unmanned-systems brigade set a range record at 215.5 km. It has spread from a few crews to about 100 military units and 250 trained teams, and one operator can fly it from anywhere in Ukraine. It also works in pairs with the SHARK-M reconnaissance drone—one finds the target, the other kills it. In July, Ukrainians crowdfunded 30 of the drones for military intelligence and the security service through Serhii Prytula's foundation.
