A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos
The Telegram channel Voyna s Feykami posted an AI-generated video about ballot stuffing. It shows a six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio, soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo, and the alien from Ridley Scott’s film “Alien” dropping ballots into a ballot box. A voice-over warns that videos purporting to show election violations may have been generated using AI.
“Stay alert! In the coming days, as the election approaches, pressure on Russians will mount. Don’t believe everything you see online,” the channel says in the post accompanying the video. The channel urges readers to rely “only on official sources” for information about the election.
By the time this article was published, the video featuring DiCaprio had been viewed more than 100,000 times and shared by several other Telegram channels.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.
Voyna s Feykami is run by Dialog, an autonomous nonprofit organization established by the Moscow authorities in 2019 as an online “citizen feedback” center. As Proekt reported, Dialog was actually tasked with promoting political advertising ahead of the vote on constitutional amendments. During the pandemic, Dialog was also responsible for providing information about the coronavirus. After Russia criminalized spreading false information about the virus, the organization began searching for such content.
The organization’s responsibilities expanded after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dialog employees handled communications for the Defense Ministry and also fabricated stories about Ukraine. During this period, Dialog launched the Voyna s Feykami Telegram channel and a website of the same name.
In 2023, Meduza, iStories, and The Bell published a joint investigation into Dialog’s work. We found that Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of Russia’s Presidential Administration, oversees the organization on the Kremlin’s behalf. Sources described Vladimir Tabak, who has headed Dialog since 2021, as “Surkov’s man,” whom Kiriyenko had “inherited” along with his position. According to the sources, Kiriyenko personally visited the organization’s office to celebrate their victory in the vote on the constitutional amendments.
The journalists also examined Dialog’s internal guidelines for “debunking fake news.” When there is no basis whatsoever for refuting a story, the guidelines instruct employees to discredit the source, point out that the report contains no photos or videos, or suggest who might benefit from spreading it.
Voyna s Feykami has claimed, for example, that Ukrainian air defenses caused a gas explosion — not a Russian missile strike — that killed 46 people in an apartment building in Dnipro. articles.title: Meduza found Russia’s unpublished anti-extremism plan on a school website. It calls for identifying ‘Russophobes’ in the military and using AI for propaganda.
articles.body:
Meduza found Russia’s unpublished anti-extremism plan on a school website. It calls for identifying ‘Russophobes’ in the military and using AI for propaganda.
Meduza found a publicly accessible copy of the unpublished “Action Plan for Implementing the Russian Federation’s Strategy for Countering Extremism.” Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko approved the plan in March 2025. The document was never officially published, but the authors of related regional and municipal plans cited a draft with the same title and reference number (No. DCh-P44-10219).
Vladimir Putin approved the strategy itself in December 2024. It details what the Kremlin considers the main “extremist” threats and how it intends to combat them. The action plan spells out the authorities’ next steps. But Meduza found that it sometimes goes far beyond the original document.
We found the plan in an unexpected place. The file, marked “for official use only,” appeared six months ago on the website of a school in the village of Leningradskaya, in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai, hosted on the gosuslugi.ru domain. On March 10–11, roughly a dozen other documents were uploaded to the same site. They included both the school’s internal plan for preventing extremism and terrorism and a comprehensive federal plan for countering terrorist ideology in 2024–2028. The latter was drafted by the head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and approved by the Russian president. It had been published before, but the school had a version bearing the signatures of Alexander Bortnikov and Vladimir Putin.
Is this document authentic?
Circumstantial evidence suggests the document is probably authentic, though we cannot be completely certain.
In theory, the electronic signature could be used to verify its authenticity, and there was reason to hope this would be possible. The first page bears a stamp reading, “Document signed electronically.” It also lists the signature’s identifier (00BC60EF36970905F3079D8DDD28705EBF), its validity period (April 23, 2024, to July 17, 2025), and its holder (Dmitry Chernyshenko). However, we do not know how to locate the signature itself.
For comparison, extracts from Russia’s Unified State Register of Legal Entities bear a similar notation, but their signatures are embedded in the files. The document we examined contains no embedded signature, though it could theoretically be stored in a separate external file. If you understand the intricacies of Russian government document management, please write to us.
We did, however, find an identical stamp with the same holder, identifier, and validity period in a government-issued assignment for Moscow State University published on the university’s website.
The federal plan we examined contains 77 items, each identifying the agencies responsible for that measure. The document does not describe in detail the steps proposed to implement the updated strategy for countering extremism, so the context of some initiatives may not be entirely clear. But the authorities appear to have identified specific phenomena and challenges they intend to tackle first, rather than abstract threats. Here is a look at the dangers the Kremlin sees — and where.
Russophobia was declared a new threat, but officials plan to look for it only in the military and security agencies
20. Taking measures to prevent and suppress Russophobia, xenophobia, radicalism, and extremism among military personnel and civilian staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, the National Guard of the Russian Federation, the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation, and the Interior Ministry of the Russian Federation.
The strategy for countering extremism defined Russophobia as follows:
An unfriendly, prejudiced, or hostile attitude toward Russian citizens, the Russian language and culture, and Russian traditions and history, expressed, among other things, in the aggressive attitudes and actions of political forces and their individual representatives, as well as discriminatory actions by the authorities of unfriendly states against Russia;
The strategy also linked Russophobia to the war in Ukraine. Putin accused unfriendly states of using the “Ukraine crisis” to “stoke aggressive Russophobic sentiment around the world.”
But judging by the action plan Meduza examined, one of the following must be true:
- Either Russophobia has been found only within the Defense Ministry, the National Guard, the FSB, and the Interior Ministry
- Or combating other Russophobes is much harder, if not impossible
- Or the federal authorities do not actually consider this fight a priority
Officials plan to look specifically for extremists among conscripts and contract soldiers
21. Taking joint measures, including through military enlistment offices and contract-service recruitment centers, to gather information on whether draft-age citizens and people signing military contracts are involved in the activities of extremist organizations.
The Defense Ministry, the National Guard, the Interior Ministry, and the FSB were assigned this task.
The strategy itself makes no mention of conscripts, contract soldiers, military enlistment offices, or even the Defense Ministry.
And among sports coaches, too
6. Taking legislative measures to prevent adherents of extremist ideology from infiltrating the sports sector, including the coaching and teaching staffs of sports schools and clubs.
The strategy describes a similar problem but focuses on combat sports:
The spread of radicalism in the sports community, including in sports schools and combat sports clubs, as well as the infiltration of coaching and instructional staff by adherents of extremist ideology, is a serious cause for concern.
The new wording could formally apply to every kind of sports school, including figure skating and chess schools.
In December 2025, it emerged that the authorities planned to create a single registry of coaches. Putin instructed the government to determine how the Sports Ministry would compile the registry, who would have access to the information, and how that access would work. The government had until April 15, 2026, to complete the task. It is unclear whether the cabinet met the deadline: no documents concerning the system’s launch are publicly available.
We do not know whether this initiative is related to the anti-extremism action plan. But we found no other “legislative measures.”
Ethnic and religious organized crime groups have apparently managed to corrupt parts of the government
13. Identifying and disrupting corrupt ties between organized criminal groups, including those formed along ethnic and religious lines, and state or local government bodies, and preventing these groups from financing extremist activity.
The strategy itself makes no mention of corruption or organized criminal groups — much less groups formed “along ethnic and religious lines.” It is unclear which religions this refers to. The law “On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations” lists only the following religions as forming “an integral part of the historical heritage of the peoples of Russia”:
- Christianity
- Islam
- Buddhism
- Judaism
Enemy number one Russia’s new national security strategy faces off against the US and threats to ‘spiritual values’
Further reading
The authorities believe residents of Ukraine’s occupied territories lack “traditional” Russian values
61. Taking measures to promote the smooth social and cultural integration into Russian society of residents of the Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics and the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, as well as people who have moved permanently from these territories to other regions of Russia, in order to prevent the social and political situation from deteriorating. Involving them in volunteer work and other activities that benefit society to instill in them traditional Russian spiritual and moral values.
The strategy itself already called for integrating residents of the occupied parts of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions. But the action plan indicates that they lack “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values” — values that still have to be instilled in them. A presidential decree issued in November 2022 established the following list of traditional values:
- Life
- Dignity
- Human rights and freedoms
- Patriotism
- Civic-mindedness
- Service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate
- High moral ideals
- Strong families
- Productive work
- The primacy of the spiritual over the material
- Humanism
- Compassion
- Justice
- Collectivism
- Mutual assistance and mutual respect
- Historical memory and continuity between generations
- The unity of Russia’s peoples
So what do they have instead of these values? Of course, the authorities did not forget about “neo-Nazism and Ukrainian nationalism”
12. Ensuring cooperation among entities involved in countering extremism in border territories and the territories of the Russian Federation’s new constituent regions in order to prevent members of international extremist and terrorist organizations from entering the Russian Federation. Implementing coordinated measures aimed at preventing and suppressing the spread of extremist ideology in the new constituent regions of the Russian Federation, primarily neo-Nazism and Ukrainian nationalism.
The plan envisioned using AI for anti-extremism propaganda
45. Developing proposals for using artificial intelligence and big-data processing technologies to monitor media outlets and information and telecommunications networks, including the Internet; conduct streaming data analysis; identify anonymous participants in extremist activity; and prepare and distribute informational materials on preventing and suppressing extremist activity, with the aim of making Russian citizens more vigilant and encouraging them to take an interest in countering extremism.
The strategy itself already mentioned plans to use artificial intelligence to identify anonymous “extremists” and monitor publications. The plan retained this wording verbatim but added plans to use AI for propaganda. It is unclear exactly what the Digital Development Ministry, the federal media regulator Roskomnadzor, the Interior Ministry, and the FSB were being asked to do. The first thing that comes to mind is generating AI slop for social media.

articles.title: Russia-installed officials in occupied Sevastopol begin seizing property from owners with relatives in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia-installed authorities in illegally annexed Sevastopol have begun confiscating property based in part on owners’ family ties to Ukraine. A new list of property earmarked for seizure includes assets linked to the wife of a Ukrainian judge, a company whose director’s son serves in Ukraine’s armed forces, and a businessman whose father was described by authorities as a former Ukrainian serviceman. In another case, occupation authorities publicly cited only the owner’s Ukrainian citizenship as grounds for confiscation.
The Russia-installed government of Sevastopol adopted a resolution on Sept. 15 transferring such property to the city treasury. The list includes six companies and five individuals whose assets were taken. Russia-appointed governor Mikhail Razvozhayev said the cases were reviewed by a working group of the local Anti-Terrorism Commission together with Russia’s financial monitoring agency Rosfinmonitoring, the FSB, and other government bodies.
The authorities claim that everyone on the list either helped Ukraine’s armed forces or acted “to the detriment of Russia’s security.”
However, Razvozhayev’s own explanations justifying the confiscations show that the grounds vary widely, from alleged transfers of information about Russian military personnel to simply having relatives in Ukraine.
The most striking case involves 56-year-old Olena Vasylenko. Razvozhayev said she is the wife of a judge on the Sixth Administrative Court of Appeal in Kyiv and that apartments in one of Sevastopol’s apartment buildings are registered in her name. The official did not state any other accusations against Vasylenko and did not allege that she had transferred money to Ukraine’s armed forces, nor that she cooperated with Ukrainian intelligence services or passed any information to Ukraine. There have been no reports of a criminal case against her.
Nevertheless, Vasylenko’s real estate was transferred to the city treasury alongside the property of people whom the Russian security services accuse of treason.
A relative serving in Ukraine’s armed forces was also cited to justify the seizure of property belonging to Rifer LLC. Since 2015, the company has been headed by a man identified as A.B. Authorities said he holds an “anti-Russian position” but did not explain what that meant.
They did, however, specifically note that Gerashchenko’s son serves in Ukraine’s armed forces. Razvozhayev did not say that Gerashchenko himself or his company had transferred money to the Ukrainian military or provided it with other assistance.
A local businessman with a father in Kyiv
The Russian authorities linked three other companies — KETZ Saturn, Atlantis-LTD, and Rosttrade — to Sevastopol businessman Viktor Rozhmanov. Officials also made accusations against Rozhmanov personally, with the Russian Anti-Terrorism Commission saying he belongs to “pro-Ukrainian groups,” spreads information supporting Ukraine’s armed forces, and posts content that Russian authorities consider to be “discrediting” to the Russian military. The authorities did not cite any specific posts.
Another allegation concerned Rozhmanov’s relationship with his father. Russia-appointed Sevastopol governor Razvozhayev said the businessman’s father is a former member of Ukraine’s armed forces who lives in Kyiv. Through him, Rozhmanov allegedly “maintains contacts with representatives of the Ukrainian regime.”
The Insider found no previous reports accusing Rozhmanov of supporting the Armed Forces of Ukraine or of having ties to Ukrainian authorities. Those purported connections became public only when the decision to seize his assets was announced.
The Rozhmanov family’s connection to Kyiv, however, can be traced through older Russian court records. Arbitration cases involving Saturn and Atlantis mention the businessman’s father, Vitaly Gennadievich Rozhmanov. One document says that a 2018 power of attorney listed his registered residence as Kyiv.
Still, The Insider found no open-source confirmation that the elder Rozhmanov served in Ukraine’s armed forces nor that his son communicated with Ukrainian authorities through him.
Viktor Rozhmanov himself had long been part of Sevastopol’s Russian business establishment. The website of the Sevastopol Entrepreneurs Council lists him as a board member and director of Atlantis-LTD. He also heads the council’s committee on small and medium-sized business and the development of youth entrepreneurship.
Authorities also cited a family connection to a Ukrainian intelligence officer in the case of 72-year-old Viktor Piskunov. Russian officials say his son-in-law works for Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR.In this case, however, the accusations go beyond the family relationship. Authorities allege that Piskunov regularly sent his son-in-law money earned from renting out an apartment, and a criminal case has been opened against him under a statute on the illegal trafficking of explosives. Governor Razvozhayev did not explain why the alleged money transfers to a relative were connected to that charge.
Authorities disclosed even less about Andrei Krivobokov, born in 1972. In his general description, Razvozhayev included Krivobokov among those who allegedly helped Ukrainian armed formations or acted “to the detriment of Russia’s security.” However, when discussing Krivobokov specifically, the governor said only that he is a Ukrainian citizen. Authorities did not publicly say what actions led to the confiscation of his property, and there was no mention of a criminal case against him.
Not everyone on the latest list had property seized because of relatives or formal connections to Ukraine. The same resolution includes the names of Yevhen and Svitlana Kharchenko, a married couple facing much more serious accusations from the Russian security services. According to the FSB, the couple began cooperating with Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) in February 2024 and passed it information about the locations of Black Sea Fleet ships, as well as routes used by Russian troops and military equipment. The Russian authorities say the information could have been used to prepare missile strikes and acts of sabotage.
The Kharchenkos face a criminal case on treason charges, meaning the property of people accused of directly working for Ukrainian intelligence was placed on the same list as apartments belonging to a woman whose husband is a judge in Kyiv.
Among the companies whose property was seized Sept. 15 was the Sevastopol instrument-making plant Parus. The Russia-installed officials claim the company is controlled by people in Cyprus, France, and Luxembourg, and that its main beneficiary is a man identified as A.A. Dreyev. The Anti-Terrorism Commission alleges that the plant is linked to Ukrainian foundations that finance the country’s military. Authorities did not name the foundations or provide details of any money transfers.
Another company, TBI LLC, is effectively owned by Ukrainian citizen G.K. Lutsai, founder of Kyiv-based Interrybflot, according to the commission. Authorities say Lutsai publicly stated that “Interrybflot helps the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
Property seized without a court conviction
Confiscations of this kind do not require Russian authorities to obtain a criminal conviction against the property owner. Instead, they use a special mechanism introduced after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014.
The framework is based on Sevastopol government Resolution No. 123-PP, adopted Feb. 28, 2015. The document was originally titled “On Certain Issues of Property Nationalization.” In 2024, it was renamed “On Issues of Managing the Property of the City of Sevastopol” and amended to include provisions on “terrorism prevention.”
The process works as follows: security agencies and other government bodies collect information, the Anti-Terrorism Commission reviews it, and the Sevastopol government then issues a resolution placing the property into the city treasury. There is no requirement to wait for a court to find the owner guilty of a crime.
In the current list, criminal cases are mentioned only for some of those affected. Razvozhayev did not report the existence of such cases against Vasilenko, Krivobokov, Rozhmanov, or Gerashchenko.
Earlier seizures focused mainly on financing Ukraine
Sevastopol has used the mechanism for several years, but authorities previously justified the largest confiscations primarily by alleging financial support for Ukraine or direct ties between owners and Ukrainian institutions.
For example, in October 2024, the city seized Sevastopolgaz PJSC. Razvozhayev said at the time that the company’s profits had been routed through a chain of front people to Ukrainian businessmen who financed Ukraine’s armed forces.
In March 2025, authorities seized seven businesses and property belonging to 13 people connected to the Kozlovsky-Miroshnikov family. The assets included the Mayak marine lighting plant and the companies Plosk, Tinos, Tekhnotron, and Technical Operations Center No. 1. Authorities said the owners were connected to a Polish foundation and had transferred large sums to support Ukraine’s armed forces. Some of those companies had previously benefited from tax and other incentives under Russia’s Sevastopol free economic zone before they were nationalized.
The city also took control of glamping sites at Fiolent that had previously received a construction grant. After the seizure, they were transferred to the state-owned company Sevastopol Boarding Houses.
In December 2025, authorities seized Sevastopol’s largest local internet provider, Sevstar, along with affiliated companies Lancom, Sevtelecomservice, Freenet Crimea, Digital Innovations, and Spetstekhservice. The city also took ownership of the Glechik restaurant and property belonging to people connected to those companies. In those instances, Razvozhayev again cited alleged financing of Ukraine and links to Ukrainian intelligence services.

articles.title: Air defense downs and suppresses 131 Russian aerial targets overnight, impacts at 36 locations
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defense forces, as of 08:00 on Thursday, shot down and suppressed 131 enemy targets during a massive nighttime attack by Russian forces, with Kyiv, Zaporizhia, and Odesa regions being the main directions, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on its Telegram channel.
"On the night of September 17 (starting from 18:00 on September 16), the enemy attacked with: Onyx anti-ship missiles from Russia's Kursk region; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia's Bryansk and Voronezh regions; four Kalibr sea-launched cruise missiles from the waters of the Caspian Sea; 10 Banderol/Dan-T targets from the airspace of the Sea of Azov basin; and 157 Shahed-type strike UAVs (more than half of them jet-powered) and Parodiya-type decoy drones," the report stated.
According to preliminary data, air defense destroyed and neutralized seven Banderol/Dan-T targets, as well as 124 Shahed, Gerbera, and other modification drones.
At the same time, impacts of enemy missiles and strike drones were recorded at 36 locations, along with falling debris from intercepted targets at five locations.

articles.title: Nato leader warns of ‘most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation’
articles.body:
Nato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK.
Mark Rutte praised Britain for promising to increase defence spending in line with US demands after a meeting prime minister Andy Burnham – but argued that the military and financial effort must continue into the future.
“It is essential that your armed forces continue to provide the hard power Nato needs,” Rutte said in a speech to a specialist audience at Ditchley Park, a wartime retreat used by Winston Churchill in Oxfordshire.
It was a plea for the UK to make progress towards an alliance-wide target demanded by Donald Trump of spending 3.5% of GDP by 2035, about £30bn in real terms, money that has to be found from extra taxation, borrowing or reducing other spending.
Britain has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by the end of the next decade. Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year.
Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade.
But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election.
Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two.
Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”.
The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House.
Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent.
“We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty.
Citing “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”.
Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members.
The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK.
The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons.
Meanwhile, Canada, seeking to diversify its defence ties away from the US, has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition, prime minister Mark Carney’s office said on Wednesday.
The a grouping of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states is a rapid response military partnership.
Canada, already a Nato member, is seeking closer military cooperation with Europe.
The JEF comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the UK.

articles.title: Houthis claim shootdown of Saudi jet (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Houthis claim shootdown of Saudi jet (VIDEO)
Yemen’s Houthi forces claimed on Wednesday to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet, releasing a video of the burning wreckage of the warplane. If verified, the video is the first ever evidence of a Saudi jet downed by Houthi air defenses.
In a video statement, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said that the jet was shot down over Yemen’s Marib Governorate using “a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile.” Saree then claimed that Houthi fighters successfully repelled two waves of Saudi F-15s and Eurofighter Typhoon jets that were scrambled to search for the wreckage.
Saree did not say when the incident took place, and the Saudi military has not yet confirmed the loss of the jet.
Video footage released by the Houthis showed a missile crew locking on to the jet and opening fire. A missile could then be seen impacting the jet, which plunged to the ground in a fireball. It is unclear whether the pilot managed to eject from the burning airplane.
Footage from the crash site showed Houthi fighters lifting the tail of the aircraft, which bore the Saudi flag. The militants posed in front of the tail section chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
Before Wednesday, the Houthis, also known as the Ansar Allah movement, claimed to have shot down three Saudi fighters, one in 2017 and two in 2018. The group also claimed to have damaged – but not downed – a Saudi jet in 2018. Riyadh denied ever losing a warplane to Houthi fire, and without clear video evidence, these previous claims were impossible to verify.
Saudi Arabia has been waging war against the Houthis since 2015, although the fighting was paused by a ceasefire in 2022. Violence between the Saudis and Houthis erupted again this July, when the Saudi-backed government in Aden struck an airport in Houthi-controlled Sana’a. The Houthis responded with strikes on Saudi targets, while Saudi jets resumed large-scale airstrikes on Yemen. Last week, Houthi forces swept across Yemen’s western coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and solidifying their control over the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
The Houthi offensive threatens Saudi Arabia’s vital oil exports. The Kingdom recently shifted its exports from the Persian Gulf in the east to the Red Sea in the West, as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut due to the US war on Iran. With the Houthis in control of the west, Saudi exports are now threatened from both sides.
According to Saree, Houthi forces also struck a Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait and Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu with drones and ballistic missiles on Wednesday.

articles.title: Russia launched a massive overnight attack on Ukraine with missiles and 157 drones — air defenses neutralized 131 targets
articles.body:
Russia launched a massive overnight attack on Ukraine with missiles and 157 drones — air defenses neutralized 131 targets
Kyiv • UNN
Russia struck Ukraine with ballistic and cruise missiles and 157 drones. Air defenses neutralized 131 targets; strikes were recorded at 36 locations.
During the night of September 17, Russia launched a massive combined attack on Ukraine using ballistic and cruise missiles, Oniks missiles, as well as 157 attack and decoy drones. Air defense forces shot down or suppressed 131 aerial targets, the Ukrainian Air Force reported, according to UNN.
Details
The main targets of Russia’s strike were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Odesa regions. The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups.
According to the Air Force, Russia used Oniks anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, 4 Kalibr cruise missiles, 10 Bandероль/Dan-T missiles, as well as 157 Shahed-type attack UAVs and decoy drones. More than half of the launched Shaheds were jet-powered.
Air defense neutralized 131 targets
As of 08:00, air defense had shot down or suppressed 7 Bandероль/Dan-T missiles and 124 Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other types of drones.
At the same time, missile and attack UAV strikes were recorded at 36 locations. At another 5 locations, the falls of downed targets or their fragments were recorded.
The Air Force emphasized that, as of the time the report was published, the attack was ongoing—several Russian drones remained in Ukraine’s airspace.

articles.title: Trump claims US nears 'end' of Iran war, holding 'direct talks'
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump claimed to media that the US is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran and notes that he has spoken with them "directly". Meanwhile, Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei says the US must take practical steps to earn Tehran’s confidence, stressing that the country harbours zero trust in Washington.
Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir says Israeli forces will continue operating deep inside Lebanon despite any ceasefire agreements
The war in Yemen continues as Houthi advances are unaffected by the Saudi-led coalition airstrikes
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, and southern Syria
And so we continue our live coverage...
One killed, two injured in Saudi after drone intercepted
One person, a Yemeni resident, was killed and two others injured in a drone interception in Saudi Arabia’s southwestern governorate of Taif, Saudi state TV says.
It is the first death announced in Saudi Arabia this month since the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen launched attacks.
Pakistan defence minister: time to implement Mecca pact
Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said it's time to implement the Mecca agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkye due to recent Houthi attacks.
Speaking with Pakistani TV channel Geo News, Asif said Islamabad remains committed to protecting Saudi Arabia and its holy sites, adding that even without an agreement, it was a duty to protect them.
China pressing Iran to rein in Houthis after Saudi appeal
China has privately asked Tehran to help rein in Yemen's Houthis after an appeal to Beijing by Saudi Arabia following the Iran-backed group’s military blitz in the past week, according to three Iranian sources familiar with the matter.
Riyadh turned to China for help after the Houthis made rapid advances along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, moves that have left Saudi oil exports and shipping more exposed, the sources say.
China has publicly called for restraint, dialogue and the restoration of safe navigation, but its private message went further than the public statements, they say.
The sources, who have been briefed on the discussions and have spoken on condition of anonymity, do not provide details of how the message was delivered or whether it was conveyed during a visit to China yesterday by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The sources say Tehran's response was that stability and peace in the region depend on ending the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Ireland broadcaster will boycott 2027 Eurovision over Israel
Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year over Israel's participation, the country's national broadcaster says.
RTE said Thursday it will not send an act to the 2027 competition in Bulgaria and will not broadcast the show because of the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza."
Israel and Morocco said they will open embassies and expand relations established under the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords, which saw four Arab countries normalize ties with Israel in 2020.
Israel and Morocco announced the move in a joint statement with the United States, saying that integrating Israel into the broader Arab world “will lead to peace, stability and shared prosperity.” The Abraham Accords were a marquee foreign policy achievement of President Donald Trump’s first term.
Israel and Morocco face elections in the coming weeks.
The Ministry of Health in Gaza said five Palestinians were killed and 28 wounded in the past 24 hours by Israeli attacks, including three new deaths and two people who succumbed to their wounds.
Since a ceasefire took effect on October 2025, the ministry said at least 1,386 Palestinians have been killed and 4,784 wounded by Israel, with 831 bodies retrieved from under the rubble.
The ministry added that the collapse of the Saada building had left 21 dead, and injured more than 14 others, with several people still missing, bringing the total death toll from building collapses to 61.
Iran gave a Swedish diplomat in Tehran 48 hours to leave the country on Thursday after Sweden expelled a staff member from the Iranian embassy in Stockholm.
The Swedish ambassador was summoned to the foreign ministry in Tehran to protest against the Swedish decision, which is "unjustified and contrary to international law", Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement broadcast by state television.
Israel adds tender for 2,167 housing units to settlements
Israel has added a tender for 2,167 housing units to its E1 settlement expansion plan, Israeli rights groups said of a project that "buries" any potential Palestinian state.
The project would bisect the Israeli-occupied West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of a state.
The tender for 2,167 units is in addition to a tender for 1,234 units announced at the end of August, bringing the total number of housing units to 3,401, Israeli rights group Ir Amim said in a statement issued late on Wednesday.
The decision was condemned by a representative for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Thursday who said the E1 tenders were in violation of international law.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, an ultra-nationalist in the governing right-wing coalition, has said the plan would "bury" a Palestinian state.
The tender is scheduled to open for bidding on 25 October, two days before Israel is due to hold a parliamentary election.
PA condemns 'unjustified' US visa denial for Abbas
The Palestinian Authority slams a decision by the United States to refuse to grant visas for its officials to attend the UN General Assembly in New York next week, a move that includes President Mahmoud Abbas.
In a statement, the Palestinian Authority foreign ministry calls it "an unjustified measure that runs counter to efforts to rebuild trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and create the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability."
Turkey's Defence Ministry condemned a Houthi drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia and other actions by the group, calling for an end to such acts that threaten regional stability.
The ministry said the continued Houthi threat in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab was negatively affecting not only regional security but also international maritime trade and global stability.
Houthis have gained ground in Yemen over the past few days. [Getty]
Israeli election is a contest over how to continue genocide
Despite Gadi Eisenkot emerging as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger in the Israeli elections, his political agenda won't change the current genocidal course, writes Yara Hawari.
Budget carrier Wizz Air on Thursday said it had cut its planned capacity for the second half of its fiscal year by 5%, joining rivals in scaling back growth plans as the Iran war continues to drive a sharp rise in fuel costs.
The worst airline crisis in terms of costs since the COVID-19 pandemic, the U.S.-Iran war has sent the global aviation industry into a severe cost shock, with Latvian airline airBaltic becoming the first European carrier to file for bankruptcy earlier this week due to the conflict.
While full-service flag carriers have generally proved more resilient than budget operators, whose business models rely on cheap fares, even larger U.S. carriers have scaled back their planned flight schedules as surging fuel prices threaten earnings.
Wizz Air upgraded its revenue per available seat kilometre (RASK) forecast for the second quarter running from July to September to flat year-on-year, from a previous forecast of "down low single digits," after a stronger-than-expected summer revenue performance, sending shares up more than 3% in early trade.
The Hungarian airline set out medium-term financial targets of achieving €10 billion ($11.47 billion) in revenue and a 10% EBIT margin by fiscal year 2030 as it seeks to restore sustainable profitability after a turbulent stretch.
It also plans to operate an all-new-engine-option fleet of 335 aircraft and carry 127 million passengers by fiscal year 2030, up from the 269 aircraft it currently operates and the 69.7 million passengers it carried in its last financial year.
UN mission believes US committed war crimes in Iran
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US's conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that begun in late December.
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
Turkey to suspend all flights by Iran's largest carrier
Turkish authorities have directed Mahan Air, Iran's largest carrier, to suspend all flights to Turkey, a person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press Thursday, marking one of the most consequential disruptions yet to Tehran's already battered aviation industry.
Key US House Democrat refuses to clear $2.8 billion sale
US Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee, is obstructing a Trump administration proposal for a $2.8 billion bomb sale to Israel.
Meeks says he will not clear the transaction due to concerns that these 2,000-pound munitions will not be used in accordance with US and international law.
The proposal, he adds, raised questions "about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon."
Iran's Araqchi, Pakistan army chief discuss developments
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir discussed the latest regional developments in a phone call during Araqchi's visit to Beijing on Wednesday, Iranian media reported, as US-Iran negotiations remain stalled with no agreement in sight.
Houthis say Saudi strikes killed one, targeted telecom tower
Saudi strikes in Yemen killed one person and targeted three telecommunications towers on Thursday, according to Houthi media.
"Saudi enemy warplanes targeted three telecommunications towers" in Taiz province, while one civilian was killed and another injured in strikes on the town of Abs, Almasirah television said.
Lebanon, France, Jordan to discuss struggling Lebanese army
The heads of state of Lebanon, France and Jordan will meet Thursday in Paris as part of an effort to drum up support for the struggling Lebanese military.
A donor conference for Lebanon's cash-strapped army was initially set to take place in February, led by France, Saudi Arabia and the United States. However, it was postponed following the eruption of the Iran war.
The Lebanese army has now found itself caught between the Israeli military—occupying much of southern Lebanon—and Hezbollah, which refused calls to give up its weapons until Israel makes a full withdrawal.
Thursday's meeting in Paris will center on preparing the ground for a donor conference. It will also focus on the situation in southern Lebanon and plans for an international presence there after the mandate of the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL expires at the end of the year, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's office said in a statement.
Yemeni forces clash with Houthis near Saudi border
Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters near the Saudi border, with AFP footage showing soldiers in armoured vehicles and trucks pushing across desert terrain under the crackle of machine-gun fire.
The Houthis also released footage on Wednesday of the fighting in the northwestern Al-Jawf area, as well as a video purporting to show the downing of a fighter jet belonging to Saudi Arabia, the group's longtime foe and the Yemeni government's main backer.
The group has recently made major gains in a lightning offensive that Saudi airstrikes have failed to roll back, leaving the Yemeni government scrambling to respond.
"The First Division Emergency Forces are advancing on the Al-Labanat front and, God willing, will reach Houthi positions," Waleed Al-Mahajeri, operations commander of the government's Fifth Brigade, told an embedded AFP journalist on Tuesday.
AFP footage showed the soldiers firing heavy machine guns, artillery and RPGs at distant targets, as well as the bodies of Houthi fighters and entrenchments the government forces said the group had abandoned as they fell back.
"Al-Masariya Hill has been liberated, as has Al-Labanat camp, and the advance is continuing," said soldier Abu Mithaq.
Two sources from the government's military later told AFP on condition of anonymity that government forces were in control of the lower points of Al-Labanat camp, located on a hill, but were facing difficulty seizing control of the rest, as the Houthis held the higher ground.
Taking the camp would be a strategic win for the government forces, as it would clear the path to Al-Hazm, the capital of Al-Jawf governorate, just 50 kilometres (30 miles) away.
Trump to hold talks on Iran with Gulf leaders next week
US President Donald Trump is expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the Iran war, Axios reported late on Wednesday, citing sources.
The meeting is expected to focus on US ideas for a postwar strategy, Axios reported.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defenses down seven Banderol missiles, 124 drones in overnight Russian attack
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defenses down seven Banderol missiles, 124 drones in overnight Russian attack
Ukrinform reports this, citing the Ukrainian Air Force on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Wednesday, September 16, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Kursk Region, Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Bryansk and Voronezh regions, four sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from the Caspian Sea, 10 Banderol/Dan-T missiles from the airspace over the Sea of Azov, and 157 Shahed-type attack UAVs (more than half of them jet-powered) as well as Parodiya decoy drones launched from the directions of Oryol and Millerovo in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The main targets of the attack were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions.
The aerial attack was repelled by Ukrainian Defense Forces aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Thursday, September 17, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 131 targets: seven Banderol/Dan-T missiles and 124 drones.
Hits by missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 36 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at five locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, 12 people, including two children aged 10 and 12, were injured in a Russian missile strike on Kyiv overnight on September 17.

articles.title: Ukraine Suffers More Civilian Deaths in 8 Months of 2026 Than All of 2025 – UN
articles.body:
August has been one of the deadliest months for civilian casualties in Ukraine, with at least 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured, a new UN Human Rights for the High Commissioner (HRMMU) report says.
The report, published on Thursday, Sept. 17, says the figure marks a slight decrease from July, which saw the highest toll on ordinary civilians since Russia’s war in Ukraine began, topping the previous high in June.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This year’s figure – more than the entirety of 2025 within just eight months – is 55 percent higher than during the same period last year and more than double the figure for the same period in 2024, it adds.
More drones, more deaths?
The report says most casualties came from “long-range weapons,” with most documented in cities rather than the frontline areas.
“In August, long-range weapons (missiles and drones) remained the leading cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 47 percent of the total (194 killed; 1,077 injured),” it says. “Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the frontline in urban centers.”
The spike coincides with Russia’s increased use of drones – latterly the jet-powered variants – and ballistic missiles.
In May, Russia hit Ukraine with record waves of drones, launching over 1,400 in 24 hours. While subsequent waves have seen smaller total numbers, the rise of jet-powered and ballistic drones, coupled with non-stop strikes, has made interception increasingly difficult.
Russian Drone Hits Kharkiv Mall, Woman Needs Medical Aid
The report adds that Kyiv suffered the highest casualties with 31 killed and 106 injured, followed by cities in central and southern Ukraine, such as Kherson (25 killed; 334 injured), Kryvyi Rih (16 killed; 147 injured), and Zaporizhzhia (11 killed; 131 injured).
Totals for eastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv was not named in the list.
“Human safari”
Short-range drones, such as the first-person view (FPV) drones commonly used by frontline troops, are said to be the leading cause of frontline civilian deaths.
“Short-range drones were the main cause of civilian casualties near the frontline (91 killed; 727 injured), accounting for 30 percent of all civilian casualties in August,” it says.
While the report did not name specific frontline regions or cities affected by short-range drone strikes, southern Ukraine’s Kherson – sitting just across the river from Russian-occupied areas – has often been dubbed a “human safari” due to the prevalence of Russian FPV operators targeting civilians.
The city of Oleshky, sitting just across the river, is facing a humanitarian crisis as Russian forces have blocked off all routes in and out of the city with artillery and drones, allowing no aid to pass.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner called the city a “death trap” on Wednesday and said Russia has refused to uphold a negotiated evacuation deal.
Read Kyiv Post’s August frontline report in Kherson here.
Unclear picture of Russian civilian casualties
The UN report says it verified 4 civilians killed and 35 injured in occupied territories, but
says it is unable to verify figures for civilians killed and injured in Russia.
“According to public statements by Russian authorities on individual incidents in August, at least 85 people were killed and 498 injured in occupied territory and at least 113 people killed and 736 injured in the Russian Federation,” the report says, before adding:
“Due to lack of independent sources of information, however, HRMMU has not been able to verify the vast majority of allegations.”

articles.title: Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant supplying missiles Moscow uses to bomb Ukrainian cities
articles.body:
Pro-Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH says it sabotaged the power supply to a Russian semiconductor plant in Voronezh that produces electronic components used in Russia’s missiles and air defense systems.
Targeting such suppliers can hit Russia’s ability to sustain its missile campaign: disrupting production of critical electronic components can slow the replenishment of weapons used to strike Ukrainian cities.
In a statement published on 16 September, ATESH said one of its agents infiltrated an electrical substation near the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Sborka (VZPP-S) and destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the facility. The movement said the agent escaped the city after the operation.
VZPP-S is a Russian producer of semiconductor devices, integrated circuits and power modules. Ukraine’s military intelligence lists the company as part of Russia’s defense-industrial supply chain and says it has produced electronic components for Kh-101 cruise missiles, Iskander-K missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
ATESH claimed the sabotage caused a major voltage surge and shut down production workshops. The movement said full power was not restored for several weeks, causing delays in deliveries of components for Russian weapons and, consequently, delays in missile and air defense production.
The movement’s claims have not been independently verified.
ATESH is a pro-Ukrainian partisan movement operating in Russian-occupied territories and inside Russia. It says it recruits local residents and Russian military personnel to conduct sabotage, gather intelligence and pass information to Ukraine. The movement regularly publishes claims of attacks and acts of sabotage against Russian military and defense-industrial targets, though individual operations are often difficult to independently verify.
The plant has already been targeted
The reported sabotage comes after the VZPP-S facility was struck in a Ukrainian attack in June.
Ukraine’s military intelligence says VZPP-S produces components for the Kh-101, including transistor assemblies and matrices used in the missile’s electronic systems. It also says the company supplies semiconductor components for the onboard computer of the 9M727 cruise missile used by the Iskander-K system, as well as components for the Pantsir-S1’s television channel.
The company itself describes VZPP-S as a major Russian producer of electronic components, with more than 900 products in serial production.
ATESH said it delayed publication of its claim to protect its agent.

articles.title: Pentagon wants new mobile radar to track hypersonic weapons
articles.body:
- The Missile Defense Agency is seeking industry prototypes for a mobile Forward Based Mode radar that can deploy via C-17 aircraft.
- Companies must clear a hardware-based Entry Gate before competing through four prototyping cycles under the agency's NOBLE contracting vehicle.
The Missile Defense Agency wants industry to build a new mobile radar that can be flown into a war zone aboard a C-17, set up within hours and torn down again in minutes, according to a pre-solicitation notice posted September 16.
The program, called Forward Based Mode Radar Next, is meant to replace or supplement current forward-deployed missile-tracking radars with a system that can move fast enough to survive against an adversary trying to target it. The notice comes from the agency’s Mobile Land-Based Sensors Project Office and lays out plans to run the effort through NOBLE, the Missile Defense Agency’s existing Other Transaction Authority vehicle for prototype work.
The radar’s job is to provide early warning and tracking against ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and hypersonic weapons, then feed that data into the wider missile defense network. The agency says current forward-based radars are largely static or only semi-mobile, which makes them vulnerable to counterattack and slow to reposition as a fight evolves.
FBM Radar Next is meant to close that gap. Beyond fitting inside a C-17 and tactical ground vehicles, the notice calls for a design that can run with a minimal onsite crew, monitor its own health automatically, and reconfigure itself as either one large radar array or several smaller ones spread across a wider area. The agency also wants the system engineered to keep its physical, thermal and electromagnetic signatures low enough to avoid being easily targeted once deployed.
Cost is a central requirement rather than an afterthought. The notice specifically asks companies to show a path to high-volume, affordable production, framing the radar as something the military may need to replace quickly and repeatedly in a heavily contested environment rather than field as a small number of exquisite, expensive units.
Before any company can compete for the program, it has to clear what the agency calls an Entry Gate. That requires showing a fully documented subarray design and working hardware at the array element level, backed by real test data on things like transceiver performance and signal path continuity. Purely theoretical designs or software simulations without hardware behind them will not qualify.
Companies that clear the Entry Gate then move through four prototyping cycles, each ending in a competitive down-select. Cycle 1 covers concept development, Cycle 2 focuses on manufacturing readiness, Cycle 3 calls for a subscale prototype paired with modeling and simulation, and Cycle 4 culminates in a full-scale prototype and operational demonstration. The agency has not set specific timelines for any of the cycles, and no cost or contract value has been disclosed.
The Missile Defense Agency also flagged that only companies that complete the prototype effort will be eligible for what it describes as a likely sole-source follow-on production contract, and offerors will need to obtain a Facility Security Clearance before starting Cycle 1.
The agency stressed that the September 16 notice is not a request for proposals and does not commit it to a formal solicitation. It said it is not currently accepting questions or feedback on the notice, and a timeline for issuing an actual solicitation has not been announced.

articles.title: A confession that shook the United States
articles.body:
A confession that shook the United States
Kayhan, in a note, addressed the first official Pentagon report acknowledging the scale of damage the United States suffered in the war against Iran. The US has incurred tens of billions of dollars in losses and has lost hundreds of military buildings and installations.
Trump launched the war with very specific goals like overthrowing the Islamic Republic, destroying Iran’s nuclear, missile, and drone capabilities, etc. But none of these objectives were achieved, and new problems emerged: Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, the global economy entered crisis, inflation rose, and American farmers suffered losses. As the war dragged on and Iran launched extensive, heavy attacks on at least 20 US bases across eight regional countries, it became clear that many of these bases had suffered billions of dollars in damage and were no longer usable. The revelation triggered a political earthquake in the United States, prompting Trump and Pete Hegseth to deny the report quickly.
Resalat: Sending false signals of calm is dangerous
Resalat, in an analysis, warned about the most dangerous strategic trap at the current moment: sending “false signals of calm” to global markets. Iran’s diplomatic and media apparatus must be extremely vigilant so that news about the Oman talks is not framed by Western media as a sign that the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is imminent. The reasons for this caution are: neutralizing Iran’s greatest leverage, buying time for war‑planners in the White House, and preventing public opinion from becoming conditioned. Iran must state clearly that the Oman understanding is a post‑war document, and until the White House ends its warmongering and accepts Tehran’s conditions, the energy and global transport crisis gripping the West will not end. The Muscat agreement should be presented to the world as proof of Iran’s responsibility and sovereign rights.
Sobh-e-No: The Salalah meeting had already been decided on the battlefield and in diplomacy
Sobh-e-No, in an article, assessed the reasons behind the cancellation of the Salalah meeting in Oman. The purpose of the meeting was to unveil a new plan for regulating traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and organizing maritime movement in this strategic waterway. But the meeting was postponed indefinitely. A closer look at recent developments shows that the cancellation was a direct result of a fundamental shift in the regional balance of power: significant advances by Ansarallah, the resistance front’s control over two strategic straits (Bab al‑Mandab and Hormuz), and explosions along Saudi Arabia’s east‑west pipeline and disruptions in its oil exports. The cancellation benefited Tehran, reinforcing the new strategic reality. Iran now watches calmly as developments unfold in ways that increase its strategic weight in the Persian Gulf. In essence, the Salalah meeting encountered a reality that had already been shaped on the battlefield and in diplomacy, long before any agreement could be drafted on paper.
Etemad: Iran must strengthen its initiatives
Etemad, in an interview with Amir Asgar, senior researcher and strategic security analyst, discussed Iran’s policy and initiative in the current situation. According to Asgar, alongside diplomatic engagement with Persian Gulf states, Iran must intensify its influence in Yemen and alternative energy routes—both militarily and diplomatically. Iran must be the actor that determines what happens in the Strait of Hormuz. If Iran loses initiative and the control of escalation—whether diplomatic or military—falls into American hands, Iran will face serious challenges. This is not an issue that can be simplified under the assumption that it can be resolved solely through negotiations, because it directly concerns national security. The postponement of the meeting could allow Iran to take control of escalation management through other channels, a matter that is vital for the country.
Shargh: Tehran and Baghdad work to contain the fallout of ongoing regional developments
Shargh, in an analysis, examined the gradual reopening of the Iran–Iraq border, describing it as a sign of Tehran and Baghdad’s efforts to manage the consequences of ongoing regional developments on bilateral relations. These developments, if they continue, could affect the economic, security, and commercial ties between the two countries. The attack on infrastructure that serves as Saudi Arabia’s alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, combined with conflicting claims about the origin of the attack and Baghdad’s security responses, shows how any incident in the region’s tense environment can quickly escalate from a limited security event into an issue with political, economic, and regional dimensions. In such circumstances, Iraq’s investigation into the origin of the attack and related actors becomes even more important. What is clear for now is the effort by Tehran and Baghdad to maintain coordination and prevent escalation, while Saudi Arabia simultaneously works to protect one of its most important oil transit routes.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Third Army Corps command reveals a months-old counteroffensive in northern Donetsk region. Its ultimate goal remains unknown.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps command reveals a months-old counteroffensive in northern Donetsk region. Its ultimate goal remains unknown.
The Command of the Ukrainian Ground Forces’ Third Army Corps said its forces are conducting a counteroffensive in the northern Donetsk region. The corps commander, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, described the operation in a special video address. Pro-war Russian bloggers had previously reported a Ukrainian offensive near the city of Lyman (1, 2, 3).
The Ukrainian Armed Forces have named the operation “Vivaldi.” Biletskyi said that during the offensive, the Third Corps had “cleared out infiltrating forces” in several communities along the Lyman axis — Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, and the area around Korovyi Yar — and liberated Serednie. In total, Ukrainian forces cleared 75 square kilometers and liberated another 10 square kilometers from Russian troops. They also allegedly “dealt a devastating blow to the combat capabilities of Russia’s 20th and 25th armies.” This information has not been independently verified.
Biletskyi said that at this stage of the operation, Russian forces have lost about 1,500 soldiers — though he did not specify whether the figure referred only to troops killed, captured, missing, or otherwise permanently lost — as well as more than 12,000 drones and hundreds of armored vehicles, artillery systems, and other vehicles. He also said Ukrainian drones had cut off the enemy’s supply routes.
“There is a lot of information in open sources right now saying that the ultimate goal of our offensive is to reach the banks of the Zherebets River. But our operation is called ‘Vivaldi.’ And as everyone knows, Vivaldi has four seasons. This is only the first,” Biletskyi said.
Biletskyi urged people to continue maintaining “operational secrecy” and promised updates on the operation from official sources. The Ukrainian operation in the Donetsk region has been underway for about four months, but officials had not previously disclosed it. Its ultimate goal remains unknown.
Lyman is a strategically important city roughly 100 kilometers north of Russian-occupied Donetsk. Russian forces captured it in May 2022, but Ukraine regained control of the city in October of that year. In early summer 2026, Russian forces again tried to storm Lyman but failed.
Meduza’s Razbor team will soon examine what is happening in this sector of the front in its next battlefield update.
The war in photos: Kramatorsk
A Russian airstrike destroyed a private home in Kramatorsk, a city 40 kilometers from Lyman. Olena and Yana lived there. They survived only because they were at a city market when the strike occurred. Nothing remains of the house but ruins. The photos were taken on September 16, 2026.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
