articles.title: Houthis deny report they planted mines in Bab al-Mandeb
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis deny Yemen military claim they laid mines in Bab al-Mandeb
An anonymous Yemeni military source has accused the Houthis of laying mines in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a week after the group captured the Red Sea coast from government forces, German news agency DPA reported on Tuesday.
The Iran-aligned group effectively took control of the strait last week after routing Saudi-backed forces, threatening renewed disruption through the vital maritime corridor.
The Houthis have also reportedly begun fortifying their positions in the mountains overlooking the strait in anticipation of a counter-offensive by pro-government forces.
Hussain Al-Bukhaiti, a pro-Houthi Sanaa-based journalist, told The New Arab that the report was “false news”.
“Why do we need to put mines in the Red Sea or in Bab al-Mandeb if we have anti-ship ballistic missiles? We can launch attacks against any ship we choose,” he said.
Since taking control of the area, the Houthis have said they would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but continue to impose a blockade on Saudi ships.
Arab and European countries have expressed alarm over the advance, which consolidates Houthi control over the strait and comes as the waterway has become increasingly important for Saudi oil shipments since the US-Israeli war on Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil markets have been on edge over the past week as the Houthis' gains and a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have triggered fresh concerns about global supply.
The attack, which Saudi authorities said was launched from Iraq, has taken the pipeline offline, forcing the kingdom to rely exclusively on shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military. Oil prices surged to their highest levels since May following the news.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
US-Houthi talks
US officials held talks with Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend, a few days after their advance on the Red Sea coast, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The meeting was reportedly arranged by Oman and held at the US embassy in Muscat.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a terrorist organisation in March 2025 but later entered negotiations with them to end the two-month conflict.
Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has appealed to the US and UK to provide military support in its fight against the Houthis. The Trump administration reportedly told Riyadh it would not get directly involved.
Bin Salman travelled to Cairo on Tuesday to discuss the situation with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
A statement by Egypt's presidency said the two leaders called for freedom of navigation through the Red Sea to be maintained.
Drone over Mecca
The Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, triggering condemnations across the Muslim world.
A coalition spokesperson said its forces had allegedly intercepted a drone over the holy city.
Houthi armed forces spokesperson Yahya Saree denied the claims, calling them “fabrications and lies”.
“Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites,” he said.
The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, saying that “the security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line”.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a bloc of 57 Muslim countries, denounced the “heinous attacks... against the city of Mecca and the Madinah region”.
The Houthis also said on Wednesday that they had shot down a Saudi warplane.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's help and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military buildup in the skies of Marib province,” Saree said in a statement.
Saudi warplanes have launched more than 450 airstrikes in Yemen this week, he said.

articles.title: British Army moves to restore long-range anti-tank strike
articles.body:
The British Army is moving to restore a beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour capability more than 30 years after Swingfire left service, with MBDA and Thales awarded contracts to explore a new weapon system, Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard has announced.
Speaking at DVD 2026, Pollard said the work would examine technologies for a weapon able to engage armoured targets beyond direct line of sight, improving the ability of British land forces to strike from greater distance while reducing their exposure on the battlefield.
He said: “And thirdly, I can also announce today that we have awarded contracts to MBDA and Thales to explore how we can develop the tech behind a new beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour weapon system, a capability that the British Army has not had since Swingfire, left service over 30 years ago, a capability that can drastically improve the ability of our land forces to strike and survive on the modern battlefield.”
Swingfire was a wire-guided anti-tank missile developed for the British Army and notable for its ability to turn sharply after launch, allowing the firing vehicle to remain concealed while the missile was guided onto a target from another position.
Its withdrawal left the Army without an equivalent long-range ground-launched anti-armour system able to engage targets beyond direct line of sight, with more recent anti-tank weapons generally centred on shorter-range engagements.
The new work with MBDA and Thales forms part of the Army’s wider Recce Strike concept, which is intended to combine surveillance, targeting, drones, armoured vehicles and longer-range weapons into a more connected force.
Pollard described the approach as being built around “better targeting, better battlefield surveillance and more lethal long range fire”, with the aim of improving both the speed and effectiveness of targeting.
The Government is committing more than £19 billion to land warfare capabilities over the next four years, alongside £11 billion for weapons and ammunition.
That includes £190 million for short-range ballistic missiles, £400 million for inexpensive one-way attack drones and weapons, and £220 million for Project Nyx, which is intended to develop armed autonomous aircraft capable of operating alongside Apache attack helicopters.
Another £370 million is being spent on Project Asgard, the digital command-and-control architecture supporting the Army’s Recce Strike model.
Pollard said: “That’s about improving the lethality and delivering against CGS’s 20:40:40 strategy, which has been baked into the Defence Investment Plan. Now, that will be collectively a higher resolution picture of the battlefield and increase the effectiveness and speed of our targeting.”
The new anti-armour work is also being tied directly to lessons from Ukraine, where long-range fires, drones and distributed targeting have changed how armoured forces are detected and engaged.
Pollard said: “Now, these are just three procurements that will not only demonstrate how we’re evolving operationally in response to the lessons from Ukraine, but they’re programmes that demonstrate how we have reformed our procurement processes in response to what we’ve learned from our friends in Ukraine.”
The MBDA and Thales contracts are therefore an early step towards restoring a capability absent from the Army for decades, while fitting into a wider effort to connect reconnaissance and long-range strike more closely across the land force.

articles.title: Poland ends alert after jets scrambled, sirens sound as Russia strikes western Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland ends alert after jets scrambled, sirens sound as Russia strikes western Ukraine
WARSAW, Sept 17 - Sirens sounded in eastern Poland, military aircraft were scrambled and two airports temporarily suspended flights after Russian strikes on Ukraine came close to the NATO member's border, Polish and Ukrainian authorities said on Thursday.
The Polish army said that no violation of Polish airspace was recorded and that military aircraft had finished their operations. Airports in Rzeszow and Lublin reopened after their temporary closure.
"A massive attack on the western part of Ukraine — very close to the Polish border — has just ended," Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a press conference. "A petrol station was likely hit again, and our aircraft were scrambled."
Lieutenant Colonel Jacek Goryszewski, a spokesperson for the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces, told private broadcaster TVN24 a drone had crashed or been shot down around 4 kilometres (2.5 miles) from the Polish border.
Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk told reporters that the army's Operational Command had pre-authorised military jets to shoot down any drone that crossed the border.
Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said in a post on X that Poland was strengthening airspace protection. "We have increased F-16 and helicopter activity, and are reinforcing our air defence and rapid response systems," he wrote.
A Ukrainian official told Reuters that explosions sounded several kilometres from the border on the Ukrainian side. On Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train just two kilometres from the Ukraine-Polish border.
Residents of two eastern regions of Poland received alerts warning them of a risk of aerial attacks and that they should find a safe place.
Local media reported that sirens had sounded and that in some schools pupils had sought shelter. REUTERS

articles.title: A drone came down beside a Bundeswehr air base, weeks after Berlin blamed Moscow for the Leipzig airport attack
articles.body:
A large-scale police operation is underway after a drone of unknown origin crashed 1 kilometer from a Bundeswehr base, German media outlet Bild reported on 15 September.
Drones have repeatedly flown over German military bases, and German prosecutors are already treating one August find near Ukraine-bound cargo as attempted sabotage. Germany's military counterintelligence has tied repeated sabotage on German soil to Russia, with high probability. Neither the owner nor the origin of this drone is known. Russia has denied involvement in earlier incidents, some of which Germany has officially attributed to it.
Discovery near airbase triggers large-scale search
Parts of the drone were found east of Lake Steinhude, the media outlet said. The crash site is one kilometer from the Bundeswehr's Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, the German military confirmed to the outlet. The drone crashed in an open, uninhabited area, the state criminal police office said. After the debris was discovered, authorities launched a large-scale search operation in the area to find additional parts of the UAV, according to Bild.
Investigators do not yet know who owns the drone
The search continues, and the state criminal police office says there are so far no indications of a danger to the public. Investigators learned about the discovery on Monday and want to analyze any other drone parts they find to determine its origin, the media outlet reported. Only then could more be said about the circumstances of the crash, it added.
Germany will close Russia’s Bonn consulate after attributing Leipzig Airport drone attack to Moscow
Drones have been spotted over Bundeswehr bases many times
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the number of reports of drone sightings has "increased significantly" and become "more consistent," a spokesperson for the Bundeswehr Operations Command told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) in August.
"Overall, several hundred suspected drone overflights have been reported in the area of the German Armed Forces in recent years," the command spokesperson told RND.
What came before this crash
Germany is the busiest front in Russia's covert campaign in Europe. A Semtex-laden drone turned up beside a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport in August, and investigators this month named a Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal. Berlin blamed Moscow and ordered Russia's Bonn consulate closed.
Two Bulgarians were arrested over a September arson at a Munich building site between two defense-tech headquarters, a day after two attempts to sabotage the power grid that Germany has not attributed. Germany suspects a planned assassination of a Bavarian drone maker's boss, watched by agents hired for single jobs.
The throwaway agents Moscow sent after a Bavarian drone boss arming Ukraine—and how Germany stopped them
Not every strand leads to Moscow. German military counterintelligence this week attributed part of the drone activity over Bundeswehr sites to Chinese intelligence.
Elsewhere the tempo holds: Polish prosecutors have opened more than a hundred espionage cases in 20 months, and in the Netherlands a former commander of US Army forces in Europe said Russian saboteurs attacked the rail network and tried to kill him, which Dutch Railways said they knew nothing about.

articles.title: Poland plans to transfer several Patriot missiles to Ukraine — media reports
articles.body:
Poland plans to transfer several Patriot missiles to Ukraine — media reports
The newspaper Rzeczpospolita reported this, citing Polish government and military sources, according to Ukrinform.
According to the publication, the number of missiles is small. The Polish side has not disclosed the exact number or other details of the upcoming transfer.
General Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the Polish Armed Forces’ Operational Command, confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that the number of missiles that may be transferred to Ukraine has already been determined, but this information is classified. At the same time, he emphasized that this is not a large-scale transfer of missiles.
According to the publication, the issue of transferring missiles to Ukraine is being discussed with NATO allies, particularly the United States.
As the publication notes, Poland would like to receive drone and missile technology in exchange for transferring weapons to Ukraine, but the matter has “reached an impasse.” General Novak noted in a comment to Rzeczpospolita that Warsaw could transfer Soviet-era weapons to Kyiv—weapons that are still in service with the Polish army and could be very useful to Ukraine, even if they require major repairs.
The Polish Ministry of Defense also told the Polish publication that Poland is preparing another aid package for Ukraine, the scope of which is determined by Poland’s security and the available resources of the Polish Armed Forces. The ministry noted that the package will include weapons and equipment that are being phased out of service by the Polish Army or will no longer be used by it, but could be useful to Ukraine. Detailed information about the contents of the package is classified.
Poland has previously transferred several PAC-3 MSE missiles for the Patriot air defense system to Ukraine.
As reported by Ukrinform, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that Warsaw would soon consider the possibility of transferring additional missiles for the Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine.

articles.title: ‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
articles.body:
‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
From sabotage and arson to cyberattacks and airspace violations, officials say Moscow’s hybrid actions have moved deeper into Europe
Over the course of the summer, Russian attacks have been pushing ever deeper into European territory.
On August 11, military divers destroyed two drones floating off the coast of Romania near a €4 billion (US$4.7 billion) energy project. Nine days later, Bucharest scrambled two F-16s to take out a maritime drone near the same Black Sea gas platform with hundreds of workers on board.
Earlier that month, German police detected an armed UAV at Leipzig airport, while this week Nato jets downed another unmanned aircraft that entered Lithuanian airspace from neighbouring Belarus, an ally of Moscow. In all these cases, the authorities pointed the finger squarely at the Kremlin.
As Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine grinds on with little movement on the battlefield and thousands of casualties each week, so-called hybrid attacks on Europe are increasing not just in number, but in their recklessness.

articles.title: EU ambassador on overnight attack: "Kyiv has become a frontline city"
articles.body:
EU ambassador on overnight attack: "Kyiv has become a frontline city"
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová has commented on the 17 September Russian attack on Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv.
Source: Mathernová on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Mathernová said the death toll in the city of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast alone since the beginning of August is approaching 120.
Quote: "Kyiv has become a frontline city. Since 27 August, we have had nighttime and daytime attacks. The Russians struck us heavily last night, with a massive combined missile & drone attack. The attack ended just a few minutes ago… Russia launched dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles and hundreds of drones, more than half of them jet-powered."
More details: Mathernová also commented on a Russian attack on a passenger train in Mykolaiv Oblast on 16 September. A total of 168 passengers and train attendants were evacuated because of the threat of further strikes.
Quote: "I love Ukrainian trains. I love travelling on them. Today I still do, but with fear."
More details: Mathernová pointed to Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs describing Ukraine's railway infrastructure as a "legitimate military target" and said no one could guarantee the safety of Western politicians and diplomats visiting Ukraine.
Quote: "That is not a warning. It is an admission."
Background:
- On the night of 16-17 September, Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones and anti-ship, ballistic and cruise missiles. Air defence forces have managed to down 131 aerial assets. The attack has injured 19 people, including two children, and damaged residential buildings, educational institutions, offices, a petrol station, warehouses, cars and railway infrastructure facilities.
- On 13 September, Russia attacked a locomotive near the Polish border. The state-run railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) suggested that the intended target may have been a train carrying European diplomats, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign equipment used by Russia to produce Geran drones
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign equipment used by Russia to produce Geran drones
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 20 pieces of foreign technological equipment used to produce various modifications of Geran attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia's Tatarstan, located about 1,200 km from the front line.
Details: War&Sanctions portal, an open-access online database that catalogues individuals, entities, and assets linked to Russian military aggression against Ukraine; DIU on social media
Quote: "Today's publication includes lathes, milling and drilling machines, machining centres, industrial robots, automatic component placement machines, soldering robots and other equipment from Chinese, German, Japanese, Swiss and Iranian manufacturers."
More details: DIU reported that the production facility uses a VMC 1000Q vertical machining centre from the Chinese company SMTCL (Shenyang Machine Tool Co.) and an RS-1R automatic component placement machine from Japan's JUKI.
DIU also identified a mechatronic production line from Germany's Festo, fitted with a Melfa industrial robot made by Japan's Mitsubishi.
The foreign equipment is used for machining metal and other materials, mounting SMD components onto printed circuit boards, and training personnel on specialised production lines, DIU said.
It has called on manufacturers of high-tech equipment to strengthen oversight of the end users of their products and their actual place of use, including through on-site inspections at the addresses they provide. The agency also proposed that spare parts, components, software, updates and servicing be subject to enhanced control procedures.
In addition, DIU called for regular checks of distributors, dealers, and other intermediaries to identify re-exports or changes in end users, as well as investigations into cases where manufacturers' products are found in Russia's military-industrial complex and the tracing of their supply chains.
Read more: Russia's high-security economic zone: how Alabuga, the country's main drone factory, operates
Background:
- It was reported earlier that Russia continues to expand the industrial site at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone, where production of attack drones is concentrated. New production halls are being built and infrastructure expanded in the southern part of the economic zone.
- DIU previously released a detailed breakdown of Russia's new Geran-4 jet-powered attack drone, covering its foreign-made components and key tactical and technical specifications, alongside an interactive 3D model.
- In January, DIU posted a detailed analysis of the new Russian Geran-5 attack drone, including an interactive 3D model, its components, electronic component base and key tactical and technical characteristics.

articles.title: Germany to send fighter jets to Latvia during election amid drone threat
articles.body:
Two German air force Eurofighter jets fly through the sky over the air base in Wittmund, Germany on July 13, 2026. | Focke Strangmann/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany will deploy Eurofighter jets to Latvia to help protect its airspace during next month’s parliamentary election as repeated drone incursions have raised security concerns along NATO’s eastern flank.
Four German Eurofighters will be sent to the Lielvārde Air Base in central Latvia for about a week from late September into early October, Germany’s defense ministry said Wednesday. The ministry added that Latvia had requested additional support from its NATO allies to secure its airspace ahead of the Oct. 3 vote.
The Latvian defense ministry did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.
Advertisement
Latvia has experienced several drone incidents this year. NATO fighters shot down a foreign drone over the east of the country in June, while another drone was destroyed in August. Authorities later said the August aircraft was Ukrainian and had likely entered Latvian airspace from Belarus after being affected by Russian electronic warfare.
Latvia’s defense ministry has warned that further foreign drones could infringe on its airspace as long as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues.
The German jets, from Tactical Air Wing 74 in Neuburg an der Donau, will operate under NATO’s enhanced Air Policing North mission, which forms part of the alliance’s integrated air and missile defense system. Germany will also deploy several dozen personnel.
Germany separately announced that five Eurofighters and around 120 troops will deploy to Ämari in Estonia from December through March for a regular NATO air policing rotation. That will be Germany’s seventh such mission to that part of Estonia.

articles.title: While Ukraine lacks sufficient air defense missiles, the US used more than 4 interceptor missiles for each target during the attack on Iran
articles.body:
While Ukraine lacks sufficient air defense missiles, the US used more than 4 interceptor missiles for each target during the attack on Iran
Kyiv • UNN
The US launched approximately 82 Patriot and THAAD missiles, intercepting 18 of 20 Iranian ballistic missiles. Ukraine is forced to conserve PAC-3s.
The U.S. military used approximately 82 Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles to intercept 20 Iranian ballistic missiles during the attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on September 9. That averages more than four interceptors per target, while Ukraine, due to an ammunition shortage, is forced to use Patriot missiles much more sparingly, Defense Express reports, citing The Wall Street Journal, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, during the attack U.S. forces launched approximately 70 scarce PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems. In addition, the THAAD missile defense system deployed approximately 12 more interceptors.
Despite the significant expenditure of ammunition, U.S. forces managed to intercept 18 of the 20 Iranian ballistic missiles. American military aircraft were also damaged in the strike.
Ukraine economizes on Patriot missiles
Defense Express notes that in Ukraine, due to a shortage of interceptors, only one Patriot missile per target may be used when intercepting ballistic targets.
The high expenditure of PAC-3 missiles by the U.S. military is also drawing attention because of the limited stocks of these missiles. This issue is particularly significant for Ukraine, as the PAC-3 is one of the key means of intercepting ballistic missiles.
The THAAD system was also used during the attack in Jordan. Iran had previously destroyed one of the AN/TPY-2 radar stations required for its operation, so, as Defense Express notes, the United States likely had to redeploy another such radar to the area of the air base.

articles.title: US House Passes Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill, Sends It to Trump
articles.body:
The US House of Representatives passed a sweeping bipartisan sanctions and tariff package on Wednesday, giving President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed by 262 votes to 159 and now heads to Trump’s desk. The Senate approved the measure 86-11 in August.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The legislation is aimed at cutting the financial and logistical networks that help Moscow sustain its war against Ukraine, targeting Russia’s energy sector, defense suppliers, major financial institutions and sanctions-evasion networks.
It also authorizes sanctions against individuals involved in the abduction of Ukrainian children.
Pressure on Russian energy revenues
At the center of the bill is a secondary-tariff mechanism aimed at countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.
President Trump would be able to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing large volumes of Russian energy or helping Moscow evade sanctions. Major buyers such as China and India could be affected, depending on how the measures are implemented.
Supporters say the goal is to reduce the flow of energy revenue that continues to finance Russia’s war.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who worked on the legislation with Graham, described the measures as “scorching sanctions” intended to “throttle Putin’s war machine.”
At Least 10 Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russian Attack Injures 12, Including Two Children
Banks, shadow fleet and military suppliers
The package also targets Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers used to move crude despite Western restrictions.
It would sanction foreign suppliers supporting Russia’s defense sector, networks helping Moscow circumvent existing measures, and Russian officials and military figures.
New US investment in Russia would also face restrictions, along with exports that could support the Russian military.
Graham’s final sanctions push
The bill is named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Washington’s most prominent supporters of Ukraine and a key architect of the sanctions push.
Graham spent more than a year building support for the legislation before his death in July.
The bill’s passage marks one of Congress’s most consequential recent moves to increase economic pressure on Moscow as Ukraine continues to resist Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia seeking support after US declines to strike Houthis – AP
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia seeking support after US declines to strike Houthis – AP
Saudi Arabia has turned to regional and global players for help defending its airspace against attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels after its main security provider, the US, declined to step in, The Associated Press has reported, citing regional officials. Riyadh is running low on missile interceptors, according to the outlet.
The armed conflict between a Saudi-led coalition and Houthi militants reignited in mid-July after Riyadh carried out airstrikes on the airport in Sanaa to prevent an Iranian passenger plane from landing there. In recent weeks, the Houthis have made significant territorial gains against Saudi-backed forces and have intensified attacks on strategic targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia is in a “very difficult position” because it must protect military bases, government facilities and also oil infrastructure from Houthi drones and missiles, one regional official told AP.
A second official said Riyadh was seeking to rally international allies for a collective response to the Houthis, but added that “the decision now is to give diplomacy a chance.” Oman and Egypt are leading de-escalation efforts, according to AP.
Saudi Arabia has asked France, Britain, Pakistan, and Egypt to deploy air-defense support to help protect it from missiles and drones, the news agency reported.
US President Donald Trump said last week that his administration had declined a Saudi request to intervene militarily in Yemen in order to keep channels open with the Houthis. Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice to urge US strikes as Houthi forces advanced toward the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Last weekend, Oman hosted a meeting between US and Houthi representatives to discuss regional tensions, according to AP.
Watch RT’s report on the situation in Yemen, which has been suffering from a Saudi-imposed naval blockade for years.
The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast, claimed this week that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. They released a video showing wreckage that appeared to belong to a Royal Saudi Air Force aircraft.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s key East-West oil pipeline was also targeted by drones last week, forcing Riyadh to shut down the strategic route. Saudi authorities said the attack had originated in Iraq, while Iran-backed Iraqi militias denied responsibility. The pipeline allows Saudi crude exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The pipeline has become particularly important amid the US confrontation with Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The US has seen its own stocks of missile interceptors decline during the conflict with Iran, limiting its ability to supply additional interceptors to Saudi Arabia.
As part of its response to the Sanaa strikes, the Houthis announced restrictions on Red Sea traffic involving Saudi oil. Their subsequent advances along Yemen’s western coast and seizure of strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have strengthened their ability to threaten shipping through the maritime chokepoint.

articles.title: Zelenskyy's Office explains how US Graham bill could affect Russia
articles.body:
Zelenskyy's Office explains how US Graham bill could affect Russia
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, has welcomed the US House of Representatives' passage of a bill co-authored by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal that would enable the introduction of "punitive tariffs" on countries buying Russian energy, saying the measure would help reduce Russia's oil revenues.
Source: European Pravda, citing Vlasiuk in comments to journalists
Details: Vlasiuk welcomed the passage of the Graham-Blumenthal bill by the House of Representatives and said the legislation should become an important element of comprehensive pressure on Russia.
"Russia continues to receive significant revenues from oil sales, including through countries that continue to buy its energy resources... The tariffs envisaged by the bill against countries purchasing Russian energy could become an effective tool for reducing these revenues and increasing the cost of cooperation with Russia," the presidential commissioner said.
He also welcomed the fact that the sanctions cover Iran, noting that Moscow and Tehran have long cooperated in the defence industrial base, exchanged technologies and used shared supply channels, while Iranian drones and weapons components have become part of Russia's war against Ukraine.
"We expect the sanctions to make Russian energy exports more expensive, more difficult and less profitable. This does not mean an immediate end to the war, but it does mean gradually reducing Russia's ability to maintain the current intensity of its operations on the battlefield," Vlasiuk added.
Background:
- On 16 September, the US House of Representatives passed the Graham-Blumenthal bill that would enable the introduction of "punitive" tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy. The bill now awaits President Donald Trump's signature.
- The outcome marked a positive development after media reports suggested that the bill was encountering growing opposition in the US House of Representatives and could be blocked at least until the November congressional elections.

articles.title: The EU is militarizing the Arctic. Here’s how it plans to do it
articles.body:
The EU is militarizing the Arctic. Here’s how it plans to do it
The EU’s Arctic policy is becoming increasingly important amidst global competition driven by both climate change and the region’s strategic significance. Melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime transport routes, facilitating access to abundant natural resources, and creating conditions for expanded economic activity. Consequently, the Arctic is becoming an arena for rivalry among the leading global powers. For Brussels, the Arctic holds not only regional significance but is also a tool for achieving foreign policy and geopolitical objectives.
Adopted in October 2021, the EU’s current Arctic policy is titled ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’. It focuses on three ‘soft’ priorities: climate and environmental protection, sustainable development, and peace and cooperation. Essentially, in this document, the Arctic is viewed as a low-tension zone, and the primary focus is on the environment and scientific exchange.
However, a lot has changed in the world since 2021, from the Ukraine crisis to the paralysis of the Arctic Council, Trump’s bid to acquire Greenland, Chinese container ships traveling via the Northern Sea Route, and attacks on undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. In January 2026, at the Arctic Frontiers conference in Tromsø, Norway, Kaja Kallas said, “It is time for a fresh EU Arctic policy, one that reflects the times we live in.”
A new phase of the EU’s Arctic agenda after 2022
The EU Arctic policy stands at the intersection of geopolitical, economic, and environmental interests. In recent years, Brussels has sought to adapt its strategy to the shifting international landscape shaped by a sanctions-driven confrontation with Russia, China’s expanding regional presence, and the growing role of the US in security matters. The Ukraine conflict and the region’s growing militarization have pushed the EU to revise its Arctic agenda. The EU must shape its Arctic policy by balancing a normative agenda focused on sustainable development against tangible economic interests and security demands from NATO allies.
In July 2025, the president of the European Commission announced a revision of the EU’s Arctic strategy to ensure that it addresses new challenges. Meanwhile, the EU is strengthening cooperation in the fields of energy, raw materials, and security and defense partnerships with several non-EU Arctic nations – notably Canada, Iceland, Norway, and self-governing Greenland.
Historically, Europe’s cooperation with the Arctic states has developed along three key lines: economic engagement (energy, transport infrastructure, and resource extraction), the environmental agenda (climate change, sustainable development, and biodiversity conservation), and scientific research (meteorological and oceanographic studies, as well as research on glacial melting). However, the current geopolitical situation has significantly altered these areas of cooperation, particularly when it comes to relations with Russia.
The EU joined other Arctic Council member states and “key like-minded partners” in suspending Russia’s participation in various regional cooperation bodies following the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. Consequently, the EU issued three joint statements concerning the Northern Dimension joint policy, the Barents Euro-Arctic Council, and the Council of the Baltic Sea States. On November 12, 2025, the European Parliament adopted a new resolution on the Arctic that addresses the buildup of military capabilities and emphasizes the need for cooperation with Northern European partners (including Norway) to prepare for the upcoming geopolitical competition in the region. The resolution was passed by an overwhelming majority, with 510 votes in favor, 75 against, and 80 abstentions.
The resolution outlines a comprehensive strategy for the EU’s diplomatic engagement in the Arctic, covering areas such as environmental protection and security. The adopted document signals a shift in Brussels’ Arctic policy, envisions deeper cooperation with Arctic states, particularly Norway, and underscores the region’s significance for Europe’s energy security and geopolitical stability.
To safeguard European interests – including freedom of navigation, the protection of maritime infrastructure, and environmental security – the European Parliament calls for active cooperation with NATO, joint exercises, and coordinated surveillance and defense efforts.
Furthermore, the EU Parliament encourages multilateral governance in the Arctic through the Arctic Council and regional forums; this includes supporting efforts to grant the EU permanent observer status, engaging with Arctic institutions (such as the Arctic Economic Council), and expanding its presence in the region (for example, by means of the recently opened EU office in Nuuk).
The resolution also reaffirms the Arctic’s status as a region of strategic importance to the EU (considering its direct impact on European security), and notes that the EU must move beyond the concept of ‘Arctic exceptionalism’ and integrate High North priorities into its broader foreign, security, and energy policy strategies.
By adopting this resolution, the EU Parliament has signaled that the Arctic is no longer a remote outpost but a strategic frontier vital to Europe’s energy supply, security, digital infrastructure, and environmental sustainability.
The next step will be to integrate this non-legislative resolution into the EU’s updated Arctic policy. A step toward this was taken at the EU Arctic Summit, held September 13-14, 2026, in Rovaniemi, the capital of Finnish Lapland.
Key outcomes and decisions of the EU Arctic Summit
The summit was attended by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas, European Council President António Costa, the heads of government of Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Romania, and representatives of France, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland, and Sweden.
The primary goal of the meeting, convened at the initiative of the Finnish prime minister, was to formulate a common EU strategic approach to the Arctic, a region that has become critically important to European security.
Following the EU Arctic Summit, a joint communiqué was adopted, outlining the path toward an updated EU Arctic strategy set to be presented in October 2026. Key highlights of the document include:
1) Adoption of a new Arctic strategy. Kaja Kallas announced the preparation of an updated Arctic strategy, set to be presented in October. Security takes center stage in this strategy; in her view, Russia’s growing military activity and China’s strategic investments in the Arctic compel the EU to shift toward ensuring collective defense. The participants of the summit urged the EU to maintain a more active strategic presence in the region. EU Council President António Costa stated that the increase in military spending in the Arctic would be factored into the next long-term EU budget.
2) A unified EU icebreaker fleet. The concept of jointly owning an EU icebreaker fleet was reflected in the adopted communiqué. Kallas spoke of the need to create such a fleet in light of climate change and the geopolitical situation. Finland proposed building the vessels at its own shipyards, leveraging its expertise in the field and sharing experience.
3) Investments in cross-border infrastructure. The participants emphasized the need to develop infrastructure capable of serving civilian purposes (such as supplying remote settlements) and facilitating the rapid deployment of troops. Leaders called for increased investment in military mobility, cross-border transport links, satellite infrastructure, and other facilities in the North. The discussion focused on allocating funds to reinforce roads, railways, and bridges in Finland, Sweden, and Norway – ensuring they can withstand the weight of heavy NATO armored vehicles in extreme cold – as well as modernizing deep-water ports in Northern Norway and setting up POL storage warehouses along the Barents Sea coast. The summit supported the expansion of the European satellite constellation to facilitate navigation and maritime surveillance.
4) Balancing priorities. The statement noted that, despite the strong emphasis on security, issues like climate protection, sustainable development, and peaceful cooperation remain among the priorities of the EU’s Arctic strategy. Particular importance was placed on the situation of indigenous peoples and the need to cooperate with local communities in developing the region.
5) Hybrid threats. Finland’s Petteri Orpo noted that while climate change is opening up new shipping routes, it simultaneously renders the region vulnerable to hybrid influence. The document underscored the need to enhance capabilities for responding to such challenges.
Overall, the summit in Rovaniemi marked a fundamental shift in how European leaders approach the northern territories. The Arctic is no longer seen as an environmental conservation zone and has been officially recognized as a front line in the geopolitical confrontation.
Moreover, the Arctic is no longer discussed as an isolated region; it is being integrated into what analysts call the ‘Northeastern arc’ of European security policy.
Overall, the EU’s forthcoming updated Arctic policy represents an attempt to transform the Arctic from merely an ‘environmental issue’ into an integral component of the European strategy on security, economy, and technological autonomy.

articles.title: Responsible for supplying weapons to the occupiers: Russian Deputy Defense Minister Krivoruchko was charged in absentia
articles.body:
Responsible for supplying weapons to the occupiers: Russian Deputy Defense Minister Krivoruchko was charged in absentia
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian officer is accused of waging an aggressive war against Ukraine. He organized the supply of missiles, aerial bombs, and drones to the Russian army.
Prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General have completed the pretrial investigation and referred to court an indictment against Russian Deputy Defense Minister Alexey Krivoruchko. He is suspected of waging an aggressive war or aggressive military actions, as provided for by Part 2 of Article 437 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, Krivoruchko formulated and implemented the aggressor state's military-technical policy, organized the fulfillment of the state defense order, and controlled the supply of weapons.
It was established that Krivoruchko signed state contracts for the production and supply of Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, Iskander-M missile systems, guided aerial bombs, as well as Geran- and Gerbera-type drones. He also controlled the fulfillment of defense orders and reported to the leadership of the Russian Defense Ministry on the expansion of weapons production and supplies for the Russian army
In addition, according to the investigation, the defendant initiated the creation of the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies. Its units subsequently took a direct part in combat operations against Ukraine.
The evidence collected indicates that the weapons whose supply was organized and controlled by the accused were used by Russian forces during missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian territory, in particular against civilian and critical infrastructure. As a result of such attacks, civilians were killed and injured, and residential buildings and critical infrastructure facilities were destroyed
The article provides for a sentence of 10 to 15 years in prison.
Reminder
The Security Service of Ukraine and the prosecutor's office notified Russian Colonel General Sergei Kuzovlyov in absentia of suspicion over the strike on Kramatorsk in June 2023.

articles.title: Poland to Provide Ukraine With F-16 Ammunition
articles.body:
Poland is preparing a new military aid package for Ukraine that will include ammunition for F-16 fighter aircraft.
Polish Deputy Minister of National Defense Stanisław Wziątek said this, Polskie Radio reported.
Poland will also provide aviation equipment. The defense aid package could be worth €50 million.
The statement said that the ammunition for the aircraft included in the package would be used to destroy drones.
“Our assistance is being prepared. It will happen shortly. I cannot say what it contains, but I will say this: It is what Ukraine needs now. This includes, among other things, basic ammunition. This is ammunition mounted on F-16s to shoot down Russian drones,” Wziątek said.
Ukrainian F-16s use AIM-9 and AIM-120 air-to-air missiles against Russian aircraft. Last year, an F-16 armed with APKWS II rockets, which are effective against drones, was also spotted in Ukraine.
The aviation equipment Poland may provide could include drones or retired MiG-29 fighters. Warsaw is also considering providing Ukraine with Patriot missiles following the fall of a Kh-101 missile in Poland.

articles.title: Pentagon accuses Iran of trying to steal naval spy drone
articles.body:
Pentagon accuses Iran of trying to steal naval spy drone
The US military says it has attacked two boats that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) allegedly used in an attempt to seize an American drone.
Iranian media previously reported that several fishermen were missing following a US attack off the coast of the southern port city of Kargan and near Larak Island.
Axios first reported the Pentagon’s account of the incident on Tuesday. US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure to the outlet and several others, saying the targeted unmanned surface vessel “remains under US operational control.”
The Associated Press said Hawkins identified the platform as an 8-meter Saildrone. California-based Saildrone produces several models of autonomous craft featuring a distinctive sail-like structure that carries solar panels and instruments, including a 7-meter model known as the Explorer.
The US Navy has used Saildrone products for intelligence gathering in the Middle East since at least 2021 and accused Iran of “stealing” some of the drones in 2022.
Earlier this month, the IRGC reported destroying a Saildrone Explorer and released footage showing the drone on fire.
The paramilitary force also published footage of what it described as “one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines” operated by the US Navy that had been seized by Iran. CENTCOM said the submersible drone was an older model and did not carry sensitive equipment.
Tehran has previously reverse-engineered American military technology in an effort to bolster its own capabilities. Iran’s Shahed 171 Simorgh and Shahed Saeqeh drones resemble the US RQ-170, one of which Iran captured after it crossed into Iranian airspace on a surveillance mission in 2011.
Iranian kamikaze drones have played a significant role in the ongoing conflict with the US, which Washington launched alongside Israel in late February.
The continuing confrontation has significantly disrupted global energy markets, as both the US and Iran have sought to pressure the other through restrictions on oil exports from the Persian Gulf.

articles.title: How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.
The U.S. military has long relied on large aircraft like the E-3 Sentry to track airborne targets, but leaders have become increasingly concerned that those platforms are vulnerable to long-range weapons. In recent years, the Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office have been working to leverage satellites for the mission, an approach leaders expect will make the capability more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial-denial systems.
While the effort is still nascent and there’s much to prove about the ability of a satellite constellation to provide timely, clear tracks of moving targets like drones, missiles, and aircraft, the Pentagon has made some strides to demonstrate viability.
The NRO has launched some ground moving target indicator, or GMTI, satellites as part of its multimission proliferated low-Earth orbit constellation. And the head of Combat Forces Command, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, told reporters Sept. 16 that the Space Force expects to launch a new GMTI capability called Resilient Radar System-Ground in the next year or two. Those spacecraft are being built by Northrop Grumman, he said during a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
The Space Force is also on the verge of launching its first space-based air moving target indicator, or AMTI, satellites. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 the spacecraft would launch later this month. Acquisition officials have declined to detail how many satellites will launch or provide a date for the mission. The only Space Force launch scheduled for this month, according to Spaceflight Now’s public launch listing, is USSF-259, a classified payload slated to lift off Sept. 16 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The service awarded SpaceX a contract in May worth up to $4.2 billion to begin building out the AMTI constellation. The company is one of 12 vendors selected to compete for space-based AMTI contracts.
Col. Ryan Frazier, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for space-based sensing and targeting, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the service expects to have a “usable” space-based AMTI capability by 2028, noting that those satellites will be a first step toward an on-orbit targeting capability but not a full solution.
“Is it everything the joint force requires? I think that will probably extend beyond ‘28,” Frazier said. “But we are going to have capabilities they don’t have today. … We’ll be able to do things that are high-value or value-added. We won’t be able to do them everywhere all the time.”
Frazier told reporters Sept. 15 that the first space-based AMTI deliveries will provide a baseline for the rest of the architecture, allowing the Space Force to fine-tune and calibrate its satellites and processing algorithms.
“There’s a broader architecture that we need to build out for the joint force to be able to close on its long-range kill chain missions,” he said. “There’s how you battle manage with that data, how you apply the processing algorithms, get that data to the weapons and the shooters that you need, and the time latencies that requires.”
As the acquisition community develops and demonstrates new systems to perform the mission, the Space Force is standing up the operational units that will manage them. On July 31, CFC activated the 77th Surveillance Squadron within Space Delta 7. The role of the 77th is to take the intelligence collected by those AMTI and GMTI satellites and deliver it to decision-makers who will determine whether to attack a particular target.
“They will use information provided from the space layer, fuse that with other sources of information and intelligence, and make decisions about weapons engagement,” Gagnon said.
Meanwhile, U.S. Space Command is working with other combatant commands and the intelligence community to craft a concept of operations for the new mission area—a document that will describe how military operators will put the system to use. SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting told reporters Sept. 16 his team is working with the Space Force and the NRO to solidify a plan to transition those satellites to the command once they’re deemed ready for operations.
“This will be new and different as we elevate AMTI and GMTI to space,” Whiting said. “But we do have decades of lessons learned from AMTI and GMTI in other domains.”

articles.title: Von der Leyen fleshes out Carney’s vision to paint Europe as leader of world’s middle powers
articles.body:
BRUSSELS ― Ursula von der Leyen used a major speech on Wednesday to pitch Europe as the leader of a group of like-minded countries that want to hold their own against rival powers such as Russia and China.
Not invited to join this EU-led coalition? Donald Trump’s United States.
Speaking before an audience that included Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has publicly fallen out with Trump, the European Commission president spelled out her vision of Europe as a geopolitical leader with plans for new partnerships and closer relationships — the most notable of which was offering to explore possible “associate EU membership” status for Canada, in what would amount to a major first for the EU.
Advertisement
“In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in the speech at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. She added that the EU wanted to “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies. And here too only Europe ― with its size and power ― can take the lead.”
For the head of the EU’s executive branch, who’s now two years into her second five-year term, the speech amounted to a declaration of geopolitical legacy.
Coming one year after she declared Europe’s “independence moment” from the same platform, von der Leyen expanded on that idea in a speech that seemed to echo Carney’s own address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which he called for the world’s “middle powers” to stand together against autocrats.
Ursula von der Leyen delivers her annual State of the Union address at a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
In addition to offering Canada associate member status, von der Leyen suggested bringing the leaders of the U.K., Norway, Canada and Ukraine together in a newfangled “European Security Council” that would exist outside of NATO, offering a platform to discuss hybrid threats without the United States.
She also proposed that, with Europe in the role of coordinator, like-minded countries could jointly address challenges ranging from climate change to Chinese industrial overcapacity to the risks of frontier AI models.
“This speech was all about the big threats occupying European leaders: Russia and China, and to a lesser extent the United States,” said Mujtaba Rahman, Europe director at the Eurasia Group political consultancy. “It was all about how the EU can organize itself amid an imperialist Russia, a withdrawing America and a materialist China — it’s an attempt to draw those dots together.”
Advertisement
Yet for many of those watching, the speech was heavy on lofty ideas like associate membership for Canada — which faces considerable obstacles to become a reality — and light on practical new proposals to deal with Europe’s immediate challenges.
“Dr. von der Leyen is at her best when she diagnoses the ills of our time and of our Europe,” said French centrist lawmaker Nathalie Loiseau, who sits on the European Parliament’s security and defense committee. “We’re still waiting for the prescription that will help Europe regain its health.”
Skating over the issues
At a time when the EU economy is struggling with anemic growth and high inflation linked to runaway energy prices, the Commission president reiterated previously announced policy proposals on the economy, rather than pitching new ideas.
For example, the speech did not address how to meet Ukraine’s immediate financing needs — a pressing concern at a time when Kyiv has said it needs an additional €23 billion before the end of the year and the EU is its main financial benefactor.
It also included tough language on trade imbalances with China and the toll they are taking on Europe’s economy, but included no new policy proposal aside from doubling down on ongoing dialogue with Beijing.
It also skated over some of the major foreign policy issues dividing EU capitals, namely the Middle East and Israel’s relationship with the Palestinian territories in the West Bank and Gaza.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen made headlines last year by proposing to suspend the EU’s Association Agreement with Israel over humanitarian violations in Gaza. But this time she disappointed lawmakers who’d hoped she might offer a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements, an implicit recognition that her proposal from last year had floundered amid divisions between capitals.
Instead, she lamented the situation in Israel’s illegal West Bank settlements — and urged governments to overcome their disagreements.
Most of all, however, it was von der Leyen’s implicit suggestion that the EU should forge on without relying on the U.S., striking up new partnerships and setting up its own Security Council — outside of NATO — that seemed to unnerve some of the diplomats, lawmakers and officials watching her speech.
“I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras. | Denis Lomme/EP
“I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras, an Estonian member of the conservative European People’s Party and former commander of his country’s armed forces. “Putin is talking about recreating the security infrastructure in Europe and now the European Union starts to do it itself by attacking NATO.”
The Security Council was “a dead-born idea,” said Željana Zovko, vice-chair of von der Leyen’s EPP.
Indeed, many watchers pointed to the reality that in areas ranging from technology to pharmaceuticals to defense procurement, the EU remains heavily dependent on the U.S.
“So much of what we need for Europe’s defense and our economy is done with the United States,” said a diplomat from an eastern EU country who was granted anonymity. “Why alienate them?”

articles.title: Canadian General predicts six more months of war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Canadian General predicts six more months of war in Ukraine
Retired Royal Canadian Air Force Major-General Scott Clancy expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
“That's what I think you'll see over the next six months: that war of attrition, that strategic endurance, playing out. How much pain can Ukraine inflict on Russia's supply chains, people, and economy with its long-range strike capability, versus the kind of power Russia has been bringing to bear, especially around Kyiv?” Clancy said.
In his view, this is going “to keep revealing gaps in Ukrainian air defense, leading to more successful Russian strikes.”
“That means Ukraine's power grid and energy production are going to become increasingly compromised,” the Major-General noted.
He concluded that “the stalemate on the ground will continue, but the strategic endurance contest between the two sides is what plays out over the next while.”
