articles.title: “I can travel back to Finland and be safe. That is a luxury”: Sanna Marin on the Russian strike that stopped her train from Kyiv
articles.body:
Sanna Marin has made the journey to Kyiv and back many times since February 2022, in winter, summer, and autumn. Speaking at the Book 2.0 conference in Lisbon on Wednesday, days after returning from the September 2026 Yalta European Strategy conference, the former Finnish prime minister said this trip stood apart.
"This was the first time that I noticed so many drone alarms," she said. "I think there was only one missile alarm at that time we visited previously. Now in Kyiv, in this international meeting, I have never seen so many alarms going off when there's an international meeting, also with the US quite heavily represented there on site."
The knock at 5 a.m.
Marin was traveling back to Poland by train when the drone threat reached her carriage. "There was a knock on the door at 5 a.m. saying that we need to evacuate the train," she said. "I quickly put on my clothes and then saw what was happening. But then for some reason we were able to continue, so we never evacuated."
Another train on the same route was less fortunate. "Another train that was also traveling to Poland was evacuated several times, and it was also hit by a drone, and there was a missile that landed quite near as well."
That strike, on 13 September, hit the locomotive of a passenger train near the Polish border, at the Yahodyn crossing in Volyn Oblast. Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said the Russian drone may have been aimed at a diplomatic train carrying security advisers from several EU states and former European leaders, including former UK prime minister Boris Johnson, which had left the station earlier than scheduled as staff adjusted movements in real time. Former CIA director David Petraeus was on another train at the crossing during the attack.
Marin was careful not to assert what Russia intended. "I don't know what are the motives behind this. Was it just an accident where they're trying to hit a gas station, or whatever? So I don't know about the motives." A gas station near the Yahodyn crossing was indeed struck the same night, setting off a large fire.
A warning to Europe
What Marin could say was that the restraint she had seen on earlier visits was gone. "I think it is alarming that there isn't that kind of restraint any more from attacking when there are international people in Kyiv."
She read it as a message aimed at everyone who backs Ukraine, and framed her Lisbon remarks as a warning to Europe. "I think Putin is trying to send a signal that if you support Ukraine, we will bomb you. It's about creating fear. We shouldn't reply to that with fear but with determination."
Russia has made Ukraine's railways a deliberate target. It struck the network around 1,200 times in 2025, more than the previous two years combined, shifting its aim from track and stations to the rolling stock itself, and about 40 railway workers have been killed since 2022, according to Ukrzaliznytsia. Strikes on trains have averaged about six a day since early March.
Why the west is suddenly in range
Trending Now
Western regions were long considered safer because of their distance from the front. Two changes have brought them within reach, and what Marin noticed on this trip is the product of both.
The first is control range. Russia's drones are steered in real time only within a "red zone" near the border and the front, and until recently that zone did not reach the west. Russia extended it by building signal repeaters on towers and rooftops in Belarus, boosting Shahed control signals far enough to reach Kyiv, Rivne, and Volyn.
Ukrainian hackers exposed the network in February 2026, and by June President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was giving Belarus's Aliaksandr Lukashenka one week to strip the repeaters from its border towers, warning that if Belarus did not, Ukraine would. Russia has also used signal-relay balloons drifting from Belarus to keep its drones connected.
The second is speed. Ukrainian interceptor drones had learned to bring down about half of the incoming Shaheds by mid-2026, up from roughly 10% over the winter, so Russia reached for jet power: the jet-powered Geran-4 is built to fly at up to 500 kilometers an hour, several times faster than the piston-engine drones Ukraine spent three years learning to intercept.
Jet-powered Gerans now make up a large and growing share of Russia's nightly launches, and the largest model, the Geran-5, is credited with a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, far enough to put Warsaw within reach of the drone bases Russia has built near its borders. The near-miss on a diplomatic train two kilometers from Poland is what that reach looks like at its western edge.
"That is a luxury"
Marin said she had not felt afraid on the train, and drew the distinction herself.
"Ukrainian people are living in fear every single day. I can travel back to Finland and be safe with my family. I think that is a luxury."
She said she would return. "I didn't feel intimidated or afraid, and I will definitely go back."

articles.title: Von der Leyen risks fresh EU-NATO turf war
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed the EU take on a stronger role in security and tackling hybrid threats, reigniting a long-running turf battle with NATO over Europe's defense.
Speaking at her annual policy address in Strasbourg, von der Leyen pitched a new leaders’ crisis decision-making forum together with Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the U.K. She also floated a new urgent consultation procedure for hybrid attacks modeled on NATO’s Article 4.
“Our systems were made for a different world — they are driven by well-intentioned attempts at consensus and compromise,” she said. “But we need to consider whether they are still fit for purpose.”
The pitch is already stirring unease within NATO, which has bristled at any attempt by the EU to tackle military-adjacent threats and has warned against “unnecessary duplication.”
“I have seen many initiatives at the EU level during the recent years — none of them yet are really protecting member states,” said one senior NATO diplomat, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Of course, any initiative has to be assessed on its merits, but I do feel that NATO has delivered much more in concrete terms for collective security.”
The EU proposals underscore a growing sense that Europe is failing to deal with proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness,” von der Leyen said.
The security council is supposed to help the EU react more decisively. NATO itself has struggled with how to respond to Russian provocations below the threshold of direct military attack.
Advertisement
The last time Article 4 was invoked — a formal request to consult allies due to a security threat — was by Estonia last year after three Russian fighter jets violated the country's airspace. No other capital has invoked it since.
Duplication drama
There are few details on von der Leyen’s ideas. Earlier European security council proposals — which the EU has rejected — include the idea of capitals delegating some defense decision-making powers to a smaller group of leaders in a crisis.
An Emergency Security Protocol, meanwhile, would allow one capital to convene all fellow EU members in a crisis “to coordinate a European response, to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact,” von der Leyen said — almost identical to NATO’s Article 4 procedure.
Mark Carney listens to Ursula von der Leyen's State of the Union speech to Members of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
In theory, a security council could help in “coordinating quick action” between the EU, NATO and other partners in a crisis that is “flexible across institutions,” said Giuseppe Spatafora, an analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies. The emergency protocol, meanwhile, could protect non-NATO countries like Ireland, he said.
But the alliance insists it should take the lead on security. “NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda,” said a NATO official speaking on behalf of the alliance.
Not all NATO allies are skeptical. On hybrid attacks, the “EU is better placed to put in place a mechanism to react, because it has more diverse tools than NATO,” said a second senior NATO diplomat.
Advertisement
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said von der Leyen's schemes were not intended to replace NATO.
“In order for Europeans to take primary responsibility for European defense, we need to have our own defense architecture,” he told POLITICO, “and we shall do that, not undermining NATO — keeping NATO structures as they are.”
But von der Leyen's ideas pose a risk of duplication, two NATO diplomats warned, adding that allies were not formally briefed by the EU on the proposals in advance.
Countries near Russia also fret that it could worsen their security situation. “It gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said MEP Riho Terras, Estonia’s former chief of defense. “It is a very bad idea … which I hope will not have a future.”
The move also risks alienating some non-EU NATO members such as the U.S. and Turkey.
“The idea of a ‘European Security Union’ not including Türkiye, a major capable ally and a pillar of stability, security and peace at NATO’s southeastern flank, would be fatally flawed from the outset,” said one Turkish official.
Advertisement
The White House did not respond to a request for comment from POLITICO.
Setting up new EU bodies and holding consultations will not fix Europe’s underlying lack of political will to confront Russia and the need to match talk with action, said Oana Lungescu, a former longtime NATO official.
“Nations … should be talking about real capabilities and trying to harness real political will to impose costs on Russia,” she said. “How can you do that by focusing political energy and some resources ... towards yet another body?”
NATO’s “Article 4 works because it sits inside [its] Article 5” mutual defense clause, added a third NATO diplomat. “An EU ‘Article 4’ without an EU ‘Article 5’ is a consultation forum with a flattering name.”

articles.title: Indian and Russian army chiefs meet in Moscow as ties deepen
articles.body:
Indian and Russian army chiefs meet in Moscow as ties deepen
Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth is in Russia on a three-day official visit through Friday, where he will hold talks with Russian Land Forces chief Colonel General Andrei Mordvichev as the two countries deepen military cooperation. 
One of the key topics on Seth’s agenda is the availability of spare parts and supplies for Russian-origin military equipment in service with the Indian Army. The issue is also critical for the many upgrade programs New Delhi is running to extend the service life of some Russian hardware, such as the T90 Bhishma tanks.
Russia accounted for 40% of India’s arms imports over 2021 to 2025, making it the largest supplier over that period, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute data. In March, India signed a $46 million contract with Russia’s Rosoboronexport to procure the Tunguska air defense missile systems for the Indian Army. 
Seth’s talks with Mordvichev are expected to cover professional military cooperation, training, and other areas of mutual interest. He is also scheduled to visit Russia’s National Defense Control Centre in Moscow and meet senior Defense Ministry officials, including Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov, whose portfolio covers defense industry and procurement.
📹 India Army Chief Pays Tribute At Moscow’s Tomb Of Unknown Soldier
Gen Dhiraj Seth began his Russia visit by laying a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Alexander Garden, honouring fallen soldiers.
The ceremony was held on Wednesday alongside senior Russian Ground… pic.twitter.com/x67sm8nV79
The India-Russia defense relationship has expanded beyond equipment purchases to joint production and technology cooperation, including projects such as the BrahMos missile. India and Russia also conduct regular military exercises, including the Indra series, which is a part of bilateral defense cooperation since 2003.
Seth’s visit comes days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi. The two leaders reviewed bilateral cooperation across political, economic, defense, energy, space and other sectors during their September 11 meeting.
The Indian Army chief received a ceremonial Guard of Honor and paid tributes to fallen soldiers at Moscow’s Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The Indian Defense Ministry said the visit is aimed at strengthening the longstanding defense partnership and military-to-military cooperation between the two countries.
Seth will later travel to St. Petersburg, where he is scheduled to visit the Mikhailovskaya Military Artillery Academy and meet its leadership and faculty.

articles.title: Quadcopters: Israel's weapon for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Quadcopters: Israel's weapon of choice for indiscriminate killing in Gaza
Since 7 October 2023, the Israeli military has increased its use of drones known as "quadcopters" in the Gaza Strip, after previously deploying them in eastern and border areas.
This type of drone has been used extensively and on an unprecedented scale, are of multiple types, and their use has are not limited to attacking resistance fighters.
The Israeli military has relied on quadcopters in its field operations. Some emitted disturbing sounds or sent messages to civilians about displacement and movement, while others carried weapons. Particular types were designated for assassinations, either by detonating themselves or dropping explosive munitions.
Quadcopters have played an active and significant role in the context of this war, after previously appearing during the Great March of Return protests along the Gaza Strip border, which Palestinians organised from 2018 to 2023.
60 killed
A report issued by the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor on 12 September this year found that the Israeli army had killed at least 60 civilians with fire from these drones or with munitions they dropped since the ceasefire came into effect on 10 October 2025 until early September 2026.
According to the report, Israel has used small multi-rotor quadcopters and tactical drones in the Gaza Strip, which can be equipped with daylight and thermal cameras and systems for identifying and tracking targets.
It said some models can, depending on the mission, be fitted with 5.56 mm and 7.62 mm weapons or 40 mm explosive munitions.
Palestinians recently documented a video that was widely circulated on social media and described as "terrifying". It showed a quadcopter landing in Gaza City's eastern Tuffah neighbourhood at extremely low altitudes among residents' homes, filming inside homes and taking advantage of the absence of windows.
The footage reflects one of the typical ways this drone operates. The aircraft has become part of Palestinians' daily routine in Gaza, whether through its filming operations, deliberate or random gunfire towards areas where displaced people are staying, or the occasional dropping of inciting leaflets aimed at Palestinian resistance factions.
The Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor said field monitoring had identified three main patterns in the use of these aircraft.
The first involved precise and direct gunfire at individuals whom the operator could see and identify.
The second involved dropping explosive munitions on civilian gatherings and tents housing displaced people.
The third involved imposing fire control over areas adjacent to what is known as the "yellow line" by targeting civilians as they attempted to reach their homes and land or carry out their work there.
Ramy Abdu, head of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, said the group had documented a rise in the Israeli army's use of quadcopters as a tool for precise killing in the Gaza Strip.
He stressed that they had not been used only to assassinate activists or people Israel claims are wanted but had also been used to target civilians, including children, directly.
He told The New Arab that the danger of using quadcopters lies in "their technical capabilities, which allow the operator to monitor the targeted person, verify their identity and track their movements before opening fire, greatly narrowing the margin for error in identifying the target and increasing the obligation to refrain from attacking when their civilian status becomes apparent, or there is any doubt about it".
He added that the repeated targeting of children, displaced people, farmers and shepherds with direct fire or munitions dropped from these aircraft, despite the clarity of their civilian status and their lack of any direct participation in hostilities or any imminent threat, collectively provides strong indications that targeting civilians was deliberate and was not the result of an error in identifying the target or an accidental attack.
He noted that these attacks are "prohibited from the outset" and cannot be justified on the grounds of military necessity or subjected to a proportionality assessment.
He further said that direct attacks on civilians are already prohibited and are not permitted by claims of military necessity or the rules of proportionality, and Israel's use of this weapon, according to the group's documentation, violates the principle of distinction under international humanitarian law, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Abdu stressed that the situation differs from weapons that may lack the ability to distinguish, as "the decision to open fire on civilians despite having the full ability to distinguish them is not related to the weapon's inability to distinguish, which means systematic, deliberate and intentional targeting".
On the ground, quadcopters are constantly present in the skies over the Gaza Strip, including areas where displaced people are staying.
Palestinians in displacement areas see these aircraft flying at different hours of the day and descending to extremely low altitudes.
Use of drones
Brigadier General and military affairs expert Naji Melaab said Israel had developed its use of small drones in the Gaza Strip, so they were no longer limited to reconnaissance and intelligence-gathering missions but had become a tool for carrying out precise targeting and killing operations.
Melaab told The New Arab that these drones are distinguished by their small size and ability to move in places that are difficult for soldiers to reach.
He said that they have been used inside tunnels and buildings in Gaza, where they can film the location and transmit information and images directly to the control centre.
He added that the drone can be operated by a single soldier and has advanced capabilities, including capturing sounds and transmitting them to the operator.
It can also create noise or broadcast messages depending on the mission assigned to it.
Melaab also said the most significant development was equipping the drone with a machine gun that allows the operator to control gunfire with precision.
He explained that it can also destroy itself if it crashes or reaches a designated location, and that Israel has used these drones in the Gaza Strip, particularly for reconnaissance operations, as well as for assassinations. The use represents a shift from drones designed for surveillance to systems capable of carrying out direct offensive missions.
This development reflects an advanced use of artificial intelligence and military technology in the war on Gaza, as the drone now combines reconnaissance, target identification and the ability to carry out strikes, thereby allowing killings to be conducted from a distance without soldiers entering the targeted location, according to Melaab.
He warned of the danger of this type of operation, particularly when relying on inaccurate intelligence.
Targeting a building or home with a drone can result in civilian deaths amid the difficulty of verifying information on the ground before carrying out the strike.

articles.title: Russian strike in Kyiv injures 16, including two children. Drone damages residential building in Odesa.
articles.body:
Russian strike in Kyiv injures 16, including two children. Drone damages residential building in Odesa.
Russian forces launched missile and drone strikes across Ukraine overnight on September 17, damaging warehouses, office buildings, and multistory residential buildings in Kyiv, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service announced that 16 people were injured, including children ages 10 and 12. Most of the injured were residents of a 16-story apartment building hit by a drone in the Dniprovskyi District, the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported.
In Odesa, Russian strikes damaged a 19-story building and injured six people, including two children, according to Serhii Lysak, head of the city’s military administration.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed the overnight strikes “struck metallurgical and radio-electronic industry facilities, Ukraine’s defense industry enterprises, and energy and transportation infrastructure facilities in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and the Odesa region, as well as naval vessels operating in the interests of Ukraine’s armed forces.”

articles.title: Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.
Lockheed revealed the AGM-158 FLEX airframe, based on the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week. The airframe has a removable nose cone to let users swap in different sensors and a reconfigurable tail for different launch options.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the Air Force has contracted or ordered the FLEX or what stage of development the project is in. Lockheed did say in a release that it has invested $35 million of its own money on the idea, based on what the firm called “a demand from our customers to have increased options.”
The Air Force has shown interest in modular munitions before—in January 2025, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center published a notice to industry seeking technology to allow for its Extended Range Attack Munition project to have modular parts for its subcomponents. The ERAM is also a standoff cruise missile, which the Air Force rercently developed as a low-cost option to bolster its stockpiles.
Indeed, the Air Force and the rest of the U.S. military are keen to build up their weapons stocks after using thousands to strike Iran during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The U.S. used 1,100 JASSMs over just the first 39 days of the conflict, according to an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies in April.
Given that high usage and demand, the Air Force plans to significantly ramp up production of JASSM and its Long-Range Anti-Ship variant—and Lockheed sees FLEX as a way to further bolster the stockpile with more options.
The concept “will allow customers to quickly integrate capabilities,” Lockheed’s release states, and allow JASSM to be configured for surface, sub-surface, and ground launch options.
The air-launched version will remain compatible with all current and future JASSM and LRASM air-launched platforms.
Size options include a 206-inch extreme range option, the same size as the existing JASSM-XR, and a 168-inch extended range version, the same size as the JASSM-ER.
Both are built to give users “significantly increased standoff attack range.”
The weapon could feature in the latest iteration of a yearslong effort known as “Rapid Dragon,” which has now shifted to become “Dragon Cart,” a project to launch cruise missiles from palletized loads dropped from the ramps of transport and cargo aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17.
“As Rapid Dragon transitions into a Dragon Cart program of record, it becomes a viable deployment platform for a variety of Air Force munitions, both in inventory and in development,” the Lockheed spokesperson wrote. “While we can’t offer specific examples today, Lockheed Martin does consider all potential launch platforms in maturing munition offerings.”

articles.title: FQ-44 Unmanned Fighter Aircraft Integrated With Bombs and Cruise Missiles
articles.body:
Anduril has integrated aerial bombs, unguided rockets and cruise missiles onto its semi-autonomous FQ-44 unmanned fighter aircraft.
Anduril Industries said the FQ-44 has already demonstrated compatibility with a wide range of munitions.
These include 500-pound (230 kg) aerial bombs, small-diameter bombs, air-launched cruise missiles, unguided rocket pods, external targeting pods and many other types of weapons.
The unmanned fighter aircraft was previously demonstrated launching AIM-120 air-to-air missiles.
The aircraft can therefore serve as either a fighter or a bomber depending on the needs of the Air Force.
The FQ-44 Fury jet-powered unmanned fighter aircraft was developed as part of the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.
It is intended to serve as an unmanned “wingman,” operating semi-autonomously, receiving tasks from a human operator and working alongside F-35, F-22 and other aircraft.
The aircraft is approximately 6.1 meters long, has a wingspan of 5.2 meters, a top speed of about Mach 0.95 and a service ceiling of approximately 15 km, although the specifications of the production version may differ.
Another advantage of the FQ-44 Fury is its rapid development.
A little more than two years passed between the delivery of the first prototype in April 2024, the start of ground testing in April 2025, its first flight in October that year and the signing of a contract for serial production in June 2026.
The FQ-44 Fury is being developed as a relatively inexpensive and scalable unmanned aircraft that can be produced in significant quantities.
Its architecture is designed to use artificial intelligence and autonomous systems to perform complex tasks with minimal direct control by an operator.

articles.title: US charges five as alleged Kremlin assassination network reaches American soil
articles.body:
A US-based recruit was promised up to $1,500 to surveil a prominent Russian dissident before being offered $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target, the US Justice Department (DOJ) said on 15 September.
The charges connect that alleged plot to what prosecutors describe as a wider Russian assassination network operating since at least 2024 against dissidents, defectors, and countries perceived as supporting Ukraine.
A federal grand jury in Manhattan indicted five alleged members of what prosecutors call the “RIS Network”:
- Yuri Khrameev, 63: A Russian national and former colonel in the Russian intelligence services who allegedly recruited people to kill Russian dissidents.
- Kirill Khrameev, 27: Yuri Khrameev’s son and an officer in the FSB, Russia’s principal security service and a successor to the Soviet KGB.
- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35: A Cuban national living in Russia who allegedly coordinated attacks and arranged travel for operatives.
- Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35: A Cuban national accused of recruiting people in the US for surveillance and murder.
- Angel Eduardo Castro, 22: A Venezuelan national accused of helping Suarez recruit US residents to spy on and kill a Russian dissident.
Suarez sent the US resident two locations associated with the dissident, according to the indictment. After the resident delivered photographs and videos, prosecutors say, Suarez and Castro made the $40,000 offer. When the resident declined to carry out the killing, they allegedly asked whether he knew “someone [who] can do the work.”
In 2025, the indictment alleges, Kirill Khrameev recruited a US citizen to photograph a target in Lithuania for a promised $200. Yuri Khrameev then offered approximately $25,000 to kill the man. When the recruit refused, Khrameev allegedly proposed a “simpler job”: burning a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation. He said the purpose was to target countries helping Ukraine, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors also allege that Durruthy coordinated travel and logistics for attacks in Prague, Czechia, in June 2024 and in Lithuania that September. The Justice Department did not specify what either attack involved.
All five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, carrying up to 20 years in prison. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro also face a murder-for-hire conspiracy charge carrying up to 10 years.
All five remain at large. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow saw no need to comment without “credible evidence,” Reuters reported. An indictment is an allegation, and the defendants are presumed innocent.
From military espionage to alleged murder plots
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, its covert campaign against Ukraine’s Western allies has combined intelligence gathering with escalating sabotage. CSIS found that suspected Russian attacks in Europe nearly tripled from 2023 to 2024, often using locally recruited agents against infrastructure and industries supporting Ukraine.
In August 2025, US prosecutors charged active-duty soldier Taylor Adam Lee with trying to transmit Abrams tank information and deliver hardware to someone he believed represented the Russian government, allegedly in exchange for Russian citizenship. That case involved an American insider allegedly offering military secrets, not a proven Russian recruitment operation.

articles.title: Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
Polish military prosecutors told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on September 16 that an armed Russian drone recovered from a beach at Rusinowo carried a live warhead, neutralized on site, and preliminarily identified as a Gerbera 2.
Col. Bartosz Okoniewski, deputy district prosecutor for military affairs at the District Prosecutor's Office in Poznań, informed the agency that the recovered aircraft had been armed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"It contained a fragmentation-high-explosive warhead together with a fuze," Okoniewski stated to PAP. "We managed to separate the warhead from the aircraft itself, and then, for safety reasons, the warhead was neutralized right there on the beach."
He added that the warhead was detonated on the evening of September 15. The airframe, now stripped of its warhead, was moved to a military site for detailed inspection, where preliminary findings indicated it was a Gerbera 2 type produced and used by Russia.
The drone was located on September 14 near Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec, in Poland's West Pomeranian region. Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the recovery that day, describing the object as a Russian military unmanned aircraft.
On September 16, Poland's Military Gendarmerie reported that soldiers had extracted, examined and neutralized components that could pose a threat, then secured the drone for laboratory analysis.
The on-site inspection, as Okoniewski detailed to PAP, was led by a prosecutor from the military division of the Szczecin-Niebuszewo District Prosecutor's Office. The Military Counterintelligence Service, military and police sappers, gendarmerie officers and the fire service also took part.
The prosecutor's office has opened a case under a preliminary classification of causing an event that threatens the life or health of many people, or property of great value, through an explosion. Investigators are additionally examining the use of an aircraft to cross the state border without the required permission.
The Gerbera is a cheap Russian drone typically fielded as a decoy and a reconnaissance platform alongside heavier Shahed-type strike aircraft, though armed and reconnaissance variants also exist.
Built largely from plywood and foam, the type carries a standard range of roughly 700 kilometers, with examples recovered abroad fitted with extra nose fuel tanks to stretch that reach.
Ukrainian estimates have put the production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, enabling the drones to be launched in numbers that force defenders to expend far costlier interceptors.
According to PAP, Kosiniak-Kamysz linked the recovery to the downing of a Russian drone over Lithuania on the night of September 15. He suggested that the aircraft found in Poland might also have flown over Lithuania on September 13, where it was tracked and targeted for an attempted neutralization.
The drone then, in his account, "crossed the Lithuanian border with the Kaliningrad region and most likely operated over the Baltic." He indicated that Poland and Lithuania would investigate jointly, with the services of both countries cooperating.
The recovery followed a run of similar incidents across the Baltic in September. On September 13, an object that crossed from Lithuania into Russia's Kaliningrad region was identified as a drone.
Around the same time, a resident near Finland's Pellinki archipelago found an unmanned aircraft assessed as a Russian-made Geoscan 701. Two weeks earlier, on August 31, Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea roughly 30 kilometers north of Łeba.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia explores uranium for energy diversification
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia plans energy diversification via Jabal Sayid uranium deposit
Saudi Arabia's announcement on 14 September of the discovery of huge geological resources estimated at 114 million tonnes of ore containing concentrations of uranium and rare earth elements at the Jabal Sayid deposit in the Medina region has highlighted a move towards developing an integrated national nuclear fuel cycle and local value chain, starting with ore extraction and extending to yellowcake production.
The strategic shift aims to accelerate Saudi Arabia's peaceful nuclear programme and diversify its electricity mix, alongside building advanced industrial partnerships with US and European companies to strengthen global critical mineral supply chains.
The technical and historical characteristics of the Jabal Sayid deposit, located about 350 kilometres northeast of Jeddah, reflect complex geological significance.
The site hosts active underground copper mining operations, while recent surveys by the Sedimentary Cover Initiative have revealed deep rock layers containing both radioactive ores and heavy rare earth elements.
The development comes amid Riyadh's desire to move beyond the export of unprocessed raw materials and become an industrial partner capable of producing high-purity oxides and critical inputs needed for future industries and clean defence technologies, according to a report published by Mining, a platform specialising in mining news and international metals markets, on 14 September.
There is currently technical and investment uncertainty, given that the geological data released so far have not disclosed the net quantities of uranium that can actually be extracted from the total mass of rock deposits, according to economist Munir Rashid.
Rashid told The New Arab that developing uranium deposits, processing and refining the ore, and enriching its content to make it directly and safely usable for electricity generation requires heavy financial investment, advanced techniques and high-level technology.
Rashid said the crucial issue in this process is calculating the cost of producing and refining uranium domestically.
He pointed out that if the cost of producing and processing the ore locally is higher than the prices of imports available on global markets, it would be better for the national economy to rely directly on imported material rather than bear operational costs that are not commercially viable.
Processing and refining nuclear ores requires complex technical procedures, including the establishment of advanced chemical and industrial complexes for acid leaching and selective precipitation to isolate radioactive compounds from accompanying metallic elements with high recovery rates.
This would pave the way for processing ores from the Medina deposit and converting them into yellowcake concentrates according to the strict international industrial standards required to operate civilian reactors and nuclear power plants, according to a report published by ChemAnalyst, which specialises in chemical and industrial materials analysis and supply chains, on 15 September.
Reducing dependence on crude oil remains the main economic gain and ultimate benefit for the kingdom from developing nuclear energy, as it would provide additional quantities of oil for export to international markets and generate higher foreign-currency revenues.
It would also directly reduce environmental pollution and carbon emissions associated with power generation, Rashid said.
He added that the discovery of uranium ores alongside other minerals in a single deposit was positive from a mining perspective, but that it was still far too early to determine the kingdom's net benefit before completing field studies, assessing separation and refining costs, and comparing them with available alternatives.
These field steps are complemented by an active diplomatic and regulatory track in Vienna on 14 September, where the Saudi side held talks with officials from the International Atomic Energy Agency and international partners to frame peaceful nuclear cooperation agreements and establish joint safeguards for technology transfers and securing the civilian fuel cycle.
This comes amid ongoing strategic discussions with the United States on nuclear agreements and strict regulatory frameworks for transferring technical knowledge and securing peaceful enrichment cycles in line with international non-proliferation standards, according to a report published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace on 9 September.
The announcement of the discovery of uranium resources, alongside rare earth elements in the Jabal Sayid area, is a promising indicator for Saudi Arabia that strengthens opportunities for economic diversification and provides new sources of state revenue, according to economist Hossam Ayesh.
Ayesh told TNA that the discovery represents a strategic addition to the Saudi peaceful nuclear programme.
He explained that it expands the potential domestic resource base for uranium, particularly as the kingdom is pursuing another parallel route to extract uranium associated with phosphoric acid production in the phosphate fertiliser industry.
Saudi Arabia aims not to rely on a single source but is building a multi-source base to strengthen national energy security over the long term.
The Jabal Sayid deposit occupy a prominent position on the strategic resources map because they contain promising concentrations of heavy rare earth elements, such as dysprosium and terbium, which are crucial for manufacturing defence technologies, electric motors and advanced computing systems.
This places the project among the leading mining projects capable of balancing global supply chains for critical materials and diversifying their extraction centres, according to a report published by Mining.com.au, which specialises in resource exploration and global mining supply chains, on 15 September.
But the discovery does not mean immediate nuclear fuel self-sufficiency, as moving from natural ore to yellowcake and then to ready-to-use nuclear fuel requires advanced technologies and additional processing stages, Ayesh said.
However, he also noted it provides an important foundation for building part of the value chain locally.
Nuclear energy also plays a vital complementary role alongside solar, wind and gas by providing stable electricity around the clock as a permanent baseload, reducing the need to burn large quantities of oil and gas domestically to generate electricity and desalinate water.
This would allow larger quantities of hydrocarbons to be directed towards export markets and provide the feedstock needed to support and expand higher-value domestic petrochemical industries.
The announced industrial partnerships with US and European companies in critical mineral supply chains are significant beyond the traditional investment aspect, as they coincide with Western efforts to reduce dependence on China for securing vital metals, according to Ayesh's analysis of the geopolitical and competitive dimensions.
He noted that Saudi Arabia has an advantage in this context by combining mining resources, abundant energy supplies, advanced infrastructure, a strategic geographical location and investment capital, while Western partners provide advanced technology and accumulated expertise in extraction, separation and refining processes.
Uranium and rare earth elements thus become part of a single strategy aimed at securing energy sustainability, maximising the value of mineral wealth, localising technology industries and strengthening Saudi Arabia's position in global supply chains for energy, technology and artificial intelligence.
This would move the kingdom, according to Ayesh, from being solely a hydrocarbon exporter to becoming a major and reliable player in the clean energy economy.

articles.title: US Charges Russian Network in Alleged European Sabotage, US Murder Plot
articles.body:
Reported by
A newly unsealed U.S. federal indictment reveals that a Russian intelligence network allegedly orchestrated a targeted attack in Prague in June 2024, part of a sprawling, Kremlin-backed assassination and sabotage campaign across Europe and the United States.
The indictment’s details align directly with a known physical attack from June 2024, when a Spanish-speaking South American national was arrested for attempting to set fire to a Prague public transport bus depot. At the time, Czech Prime Minister Petr Fiala explicitly linked the incident to Moscow, stating on social media: "The unsuccessful arson attack on the buses of the Prague transport company was likely organized and financed by Russia."
Despite the U.S. charges identifying the handlers behind that attack, local law enforcement’s response remains guarded. Colonel Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Czech Police Presidium, told OCCRP police are not conducting any proceedings directly related to the U.S. case and have not implemented new measures.
Spokeswoman for the Czech Interior Ministry, Ivana Nguyenová, declined to address the U.S. investigation, noting only that security services continuously monitor unusual activity.
The U.S. charges target five individuals accused of operating the "RIS Network" on behalf of Russian intelligence. The network paid operatives to conduct surveillance for targeted killings and commissioned terrorism against infrastructure in countries aligned with Ukraine. All five defendants remain at large and face up to 20 years in prison for conspiracy to finance terrorism.
The alleged leadership includes Yuri Khrameev, 63, a former Russian intelligence colonel; his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, an active Federal Security Service (FSB) officer; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, an influential Cuban national residing in Russia. Two U.S.-focused recruiters, Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, face an additional 10-year maximum sentence alongside Yuri Khrameev for murder-for-hire charges.
The Prague bus depot arson was allegedly coordinated by Durruthy, who handled logistics for the network. While based in Russia, Durruthy transferred over $1,000 in cryptocurrency and booked hotels in Poland and Czechia for the physical attacker—identified in the indictment as "Associate-1"—ahead of the operation.
According to reporting by the Czech news outlet Novinky.cz, Associate-1 is Andrés Alfonso de la Hoz de la Cruz, a 26-year-old Colombian national who pleaded guilty and was sentenced in June 2025 to eight years in prison for the Prague attack. Durruthy’s logistical support continued through the fall, coordinating a separate attack in Lithuania in September 2024.
Meanwhile, other network members plotted assassinations. This past summer, Suarez and Castro allegedly recruited a U.S.-based individual, identified as "U.S. Resident-1," to surveil a prominent Russian dissident in the United States, identified as "Victim-1." After paying the recruit for photos and videos, the handlers offered $40,000 to "eliminate" Victim-1 and claimed they had backup hitmen in Mexico.
A year prior, the Khrameevs allegedly attempted a similar assassination in Lithuania. Kirill Khrameev, according to the DOJ indictment, paid a U.S. citizen, identified as "U.S. Citizen-1," $200 to photograph the address of a Russian critic, identified as "Victim-2." Then, "Colonel Yuri" offered U.S. Citizen-1 $25,000 to murder Victim-2 with a "bottle of gasoline" or a knife. When U.S. Citizen-1 refused, Khrameev offered "simpler jobs" like firebombing NATO electrical substations.
"I am offering serious money for serious work," Khrameev wrote, adding he was "interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine."

articles.title: Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force
articles.body:
The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to help fill capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, multiple people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it.
Buying new F-16s—which would be the U.S.’s first in more than 20 years—is viewed as one way to quickly build back lost fighter capacity, as Lockheed Martin continues to operate a hot production line for the aircraft. Buying F-16s from Lockheed, which also produces the F-35 Lightning II, would have parallels to the decision to acquire F-15EX Eagle IIs from Boeing, which likewise came after a yearslong gap in USAF purchases.
The new-build F-16s, potentially dubbed “F-16G” to reflect upgrades from existing F-16C and D models, could be on the agenda for discussion when Air Force four-stars gather this fall for a Corona gathering of top service officials.
Lockheed Martin deferred questions to the Air Force: “This topic is best addressed by the U.S. government, but we stand ready to support the U.S. Air Force and its mission needs,” Lockheed said in a statement. “Our proven products are the backbone of the USAF fleet and provide the most advanced and versatile capabilities to ensure air dominance now and decades to come.”
The Air Force, in a written response to Air & Space Forces Magazine, said it is examining its options as it looks to the future.
“The Department of the Air Force is in initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program,” an Air Force spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.”
Lockheed currently produces F-16E and F models, single- and dual-seat variants respectively, for the United Arab Emirates. The company moved its production line for Block 70 F-16s in 2019 from Fort Worth, Texas, to Greenville, S.C.
If the Air Force decided to buy more F-16s, Lockheed would likely keep its Greenville production line going. The potential upgraded F-16 from that line is being referred to as a G model by those familiar with the discussions.
The Air Force today has 826 F-16s in its inventory, with 484 of those operated by the Active-Duty force. The jets average 34 years old, however, and the newest in the inventory have been flying since 2005.
USAF F-16s carry out a variety of critical missions, including air-to-air and air-to-ground strikes. F-16s that carry out suppression of enemy air defense missions are referred to as “Wild Weasels” and have seen heavy action in operations against Iran.
New F-16 purchases would drive other movement in the industry. Both Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace make engines that go on the F-16. Pratt, which is owned by RTX, announced Sept. 15 it has licensed Hermeus to manufacture its F100-PW-229 used on the F-15 and F-16, saying the agreement will strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base by creating a new source for the widely used engine.
Northrop Grumman, which is developing two major upgrades for existing F-16s, would also likely benefit. The company is working on the Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, and an upgraded large aperture targeting pod called LITENING LA.
IVEWS, also known as the AN/ALQ-257, is an advanced electronic warfare system providing radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying and locating of potential threats.
A source familiar with the issue, who asked not to be named to speak more freely, said any new F-16 would likely have IVEWS and multiple other new capabilities placing it not only beyond the legacy C and D fighters, but also the Block 70 fighters Lockheed is currently building.
“If the Air Force were to buy a new F-16, this would not be your grandfather’s F-16,” the source said. “This would be more akin to buying an F-15EX.”
The source said buying more F-16s would make sense for the Air Force, since Lockheed and Boeing are facing capacity constraints limiting how many F-35As and F-15EXs, respectively, they can build. And the service’s existing fleet of F-16s has been flown hard in the wars of recent decades, the source said.
“There’s only so many times you can do a service life extension program before you begin to lose the strength and integrity of the airframe itself,” the source said.

articles.title: A Russian drone strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv full of props from Volodymyr Zelensky’s former comedy studio, but the studio says all scheduled concerts will go ahead

A Russian drone strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv full of props from Volodymyr Zelensky’s former comedy studio, but the studio says all scheduled concerts will go ahead
An overnight Russian drone strike on Kyiv destroyed a warehouse storing props from the Kvartal 95 studio, the studio said.
The studio said the strike destroyed numerous sets, costumes, and other items used in Kvartal 95 concerts, television shows, films, and series over the past 20 years.
“Russian weapons can destroy property. But they cannot stop us. We will keep working, writing new jokes, and helping Ukraine’s defenders. All scheduled concerts will go ahead — with or without the props,” the studio said.
A warehouse belonging to the Olena Zelenska Foundation was also destroyed. The foundation said on social media that the warehouse burned to the ground but no one was hurt. It held humanitarian aid that the foundation had purchased or received from partners to distribute to children, families, and institutions across Ukraine.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said a Russian drone struck a warehouse in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district, sparking a fire and injuring one person.
Kvartal 95 is a Ukrainian studio that Volodymyr Zelensky co-founded and was part of before becoming president. The studio was established in 2003 out of the KVN comedy team 95-y Kvartal. For more than 20 years, it has produced television shows, films, series, and concert programs.

articles.title: Ukraine claims 6 aircraft hit at Russian airbase in Rostov
articles.body:
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces destroyed one An-12, two An-26 aircraft and three helicopters at a Rostov-on-Don airfield.
- Rostov Oblast's governor confirmed a fire and power outages from the strike, which also reportedly hit an oil refinery in Yaroslavl the same night.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military airfield in Rostov-on-Don overnight into Sept. 17, destroying one An-12 and two An-26 transport aircraft along with three helicopters.
Zelensky said Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, carried out the airfield strike as part of a broader overnight operation that also hit the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery in Yaroslavl, a joint effort involving Ukraine’s military intelligence directorate, GUR, and its foreign intelligence service, SZR. He said the operation also produced unspecified results in the Black Sea.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yury Slyusar confirmed a fire broke out at the site after falling drone debris damaged a transformer substation, cutting power in four districts of Rostov-on-Don. He said preliminary information showed no deaths or injuries, and that the fire was extinguished. NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-detection service recorded a fire in the area of the airfield’s aircraft parking apron, and the independent Russian monitoring channel Astra separately identified the blaze as occurring on the grounds of the Rostov-on-Don Central military airfield, near the same parking area where military aircraft and helicopters are typically stationed.
The Rostov-on-Don airfield has been a recurring target for Ukraine this year. Fires have been reported there at least eight times in 2026, including strikes on March 28, April 26, May 8, May 22, July 6, July 16, Aug. 6 and Aug. 28. Ukraine’s General Staff also said it struck the same airfield on Sept. 6, along with a Podlet radar station and two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems elsewhere in Rostov Oblast.
“Thanks to our soldiers, who make war tangible for Russia every day,” Zelensky said. “Tonight, thanks to a joint operation by the SBU, GUR and SZR, the Yaroslavl oil refinery was hit. The Security Service also worked precisely against the military airfield in Rostov: the destruction of one An-12, two An-26s and three more helicopters has been confirmed. There are good results in the Black Sea too. We respond to aggression every day. Russia must choose peace.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry had not issued its own damage assessment or confirmed how many drones were involved in the overnight attack as of publication. The exact condition of the aircraft Zelensky named, and whether any were airworthy at the time of the strike, has not been independently verified beyond the fire confirmed by Slyusar, NASA’s satellite detection, and Astra’s analysis.

articles.title: Presidential commissioner: US House passes Graham sanctions bill to increase pressure on Russia's war financing
articles.body:
The U.S. House of Representatives-passed bill by Lindsey Graham on sanctions against Russia and Iran is designed to increase pressure on external channels through which Russia continues to generate revenue from energy sales, Ukrainian Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasyuk has said.
"I welcome the adoption of the 'hellish' sanctions by our partners. The bill was supported by 262 members of the U.S. House of Representatives. Thank you to everyone who contributed to promoting Lindsey Graham's bill. This decision should become an important element of comprehensive pressure on Russia, which already includes Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure and international sanction restrictions," Vlasyuk told Interfax-Ukraine on Thursday.
According to him, the tariffs against countries purchasing Russian energy resources provided for in the bill could reduce Russia's revenues and increase the cost of cooperating with it.
"We expect that the sanctions will make Russian energy exports more expensive, more difficult, and less profitable. This does not mean an immediate end to the war, but it means a gradual reduction in Russia's ability to maintain its current intensity on the battlefield," Vlasyuk noted.
He also emphasized that the sanctions package covers Iran, which cooperates with Russia in the military-industrial sphere.
"Iranian drones and components for Russian weaponry have become part of the war against Ukraine. Therefore, pressure on both states must limit their ability to support weapons production and develop military cooperation," the presidential commissioner stressed.
"Sanctions must work not as a symbolic punishment, but as a tool that directly affects Russia's ability to wage war. This is the exact practical result we expect from the adopted bill," he summarized.

articles.title: France’s Le Pen rules out more money for Ukraine
articles.body:
PARIS — French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen is open to continue providing defensive military gear to Ukraine but is against sending money to the war-torn country.
“Given the extent of what we've done so far — which is considerable — we're saying we can't do it,” the far-right National Rally leader said on TV channel LCI Wednesday evening.
“This is not an act of hostility toward Ukraine. We can continue to train their soldiers and their armed forces, and we can continue to provide them with equipment so they can defend themselves. But financially, we can’t do it anymore,” she said.
Advertisement
Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of a high-stakes presidential election next spring to replace Emmanuel Macron. One of the campaign's main issues is France's increasingly strained finances, with a public deficit that could exceed 5% this year.
France's direct financial aid to Ukraine is actually quite limited but the National Rally has long been against the EU's €90 billion loan to Kyiv, which is guaranteed by the bloc's budget, fed by national contributions.
National Rally officials privately say that Ukraine will never be able to repay the EU loan and it will ultimately fall on the bloc's capitals to do so.
"You can't say, on the one hand, that there isn't a single euro … to adjust pensions for inflation, but, on the other hand, that there are billions for the net contribution to the European Union," Le Pen said.
While the National Rally is internally divided over Russia, Ukraine and NATO, Le Pen's rivals have on multiple occasions accused her party of playing into the Kremlin’s hands in order to undermine the National Rally's credibility. The media has also repeatedly asked top party figures to clarify the party's line on assistance to Kyiv.
In Wednesday evening's interview, Le Pen stressed that France under her presidency would organize a conference for peace that would bring Russia, Ukraine and other European countries such as Germany and Poland to the table. The goal, she said, is to put an end to the war.
She also pushed back against proposals made by her presidential rivals, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, to protect Ukraine's skies with French fighter jets — an option Paris has also so far refused to contemplate. "That would make us co-belligerents," Le Pen told LCI.

articles.title: The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
articles.body:
The EU plans to use money remaining under its €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to create a new program for joint projects with Ukrainian companies, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on 16 September. She announced the plan during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has pushed the EU to spend more on defense and build up its own weapons industry. SAFE was created as part of that effort, giving EU member states €150 billion in loans for defense spending. Ukraine is also facing heavy defense costs, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy putting its additional defense funding gap for 2026 at $27 billion.
"Using the remaining funds from SAFE, we will be setting up a new programme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies," von der Leyen told the European Parliament.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius estimated that the unused portion of SAFE could amount to €10 billion to €20 billion, UNN reported. The exact sum will be known only after member states report on their SAFE projects by the end of October. The announcement caught several governments off guard: Poland and other capitals say the Commission never discussed it with them, and Warsaw had been counting on taking up the funds other countries declined for its own projects.
The proposal would allow unused money from member states' SAFE allocations to be redirected to joint projects with Ukrainian firms. One likely destination is Freya, the joint European-Ukrainian air and missile defense system meant as a cheaper answer to the American Patriot, which von der Leyen described as the start of the collaboration rather than the end of it.
In 2025, Ukraine gained associate partner status in SAFE and access to the EU's European Defense Fund, allowing Ukrainian companies to compete for contracts and co-develop military systems with European firms.
Fifteen member states have since said they plan to buy Ukrainian weapons through the program, and Canada joined it in December 2025 as the first non-European partner. Bulgaria agreed SAFE-funded joint weapons production with Ukraine in March 2026.
The war is costing Ukraine more every year, the government says. Its draft 2027 budget proposes ₴4.885 trillion ($110 billion) for defense needs, nearly 44% of GDP.

Russia attacks Ukraine with missiles and drones, hits recorded at 36 locations
Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones and anti-ship, ballistic and cruise missiles on the night of 16-17 September. Air defence forces have managed to down 131 aerial assets.

Quote: "Early reports indicated that as of 08:00, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 131 aerial assets:
- 7 Banderol/Dan-T drone-launched missiles
- 124 Shahed, Gerbera and other types of drones.
Hits by missiles and attack drones have been recorded at 36 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at five locations."
Details: Russian forces attacked with Oniks anti-ship missiles from Kursk Oblast; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Bryansk and Voronezh oblasts; four Kalibr sea-launched cruise missiles from the Caspian Sea; and 10 Bandrol/Dan-T missiles from the airspace over the Sea of Azov.
In addition, 157 Shahed attack drones (over half of them jet-powered) and Parodiya decoy UAVs were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol and Millerovo as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa oblasts have been the main targets of the attack..
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.

articles.title: The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot.
Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), an Air Force veteran who flew F-15 and F-22 fighters, says that needs to change so the Air Force gets the resources it needs to recapitalize its rapidly aging air fleet.
“I am the only fifth-generation pilot in Congress,” Pfluger said Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “I need some wingmen to come join me. … God bless my Navy SEAL friends, and they are dear friends, but we’ve got a lot of them in Congress. What we don’t have is a lot of air and space expertise.”
Indeed, among the 96 veterans now in Congress, just 15 are Air Force veterans: only 15.6 percent. By comparison, there are 45 Army vets, 24 Navy vets, and 12 former Marines. The Space Force isn’t seven years old yet, but no former Space Force Guardians have been elected to Congress.
Of the 15 former Airmen on Capitol Hill, Pfluger is not the only aviator—Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) flew on the EC-130H and RC-135, Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) was in combat search and rescue, and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) was an airborne intelligence officer.
But there are no other USAF fighter pilots. In 2022, Pfluger started the “Mach 1” caucus with three former Navy fighter pilots. Four years and two elections later, the Mach 1 caucus has gone from four to three members: Pfluger, Rep. Jake Ellzey (R-Texas), and Rep. Scott Franklin (R-Fla.).
With such small numbers, Pfluger said, it’s harder for the Air Force to “tell its story.”
“What I have done in Congress is try to educate my colleagues on what the Department of the Air Force does and why we, as a department, are really carrying the load in each of the conflicts—whether it’s Epic Fury, Midnight Hammer, Absolute Resolve, or any of the previous conflicts, the Department of the Air Force has been there every single time,” Pfluger said.
Airpower, Pfluger said, is uniquely capable of providing strategic effects. But modernization—and the resources that go along with it—is desperately needed.
We … need the help to make the case that while we are the oldest and the smallest, it’s not too late. We can recapitalize,” Pfluger said, lamenting that budget increases cannot be split evenly among the services if the Air Force is to shoulder much of the operational load.
More Airmen in Congress would help him make the case to other lawmakers, Pfluger said. For now, he gets help from Representatives and Senators who represent key Air Force installations. But he also urged Air Force leaders to make their case to Congress.
“We need Air Force leaders to be bold,” Pfluger said. “We need you to be bold to tell the truth, to say we’re underfunded.”
Multiyear Procurement
While the Air Force needs to make its case to Congress, Congress can help the Air Force by not only providing more resources, but making those resources more consistent.
Pentagon officials frequently decry the effects of continuing resolutions and government shutdowns when lawmakers fail to pass appropriations on time.
A more “predictable environment” is important, Pfluger agreed. One way to do that is multiyear procurement authorities—letting the Pentagon award contracts for multiple years instead of being reliant on annual cycles. Congress must approve any and all programs for which Pentagon wants to use multiyear procurement.
Defense officials say multiyear procurement saves the government money by locking in lower prices and helps industry by providing a stable demand signal. In the past, lawmakers have raised concerns about oversight, but they have grown increasingly open to granting more authorities.
Congress has already implemented multiyear procurement for a range of munitions programs, but members of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees have voted to authorize it for the F-35 and F-15EX as part of the 2027 defense policy bill. That bill is still pending, but Pfluger projected confidence that expanded multiyear procurement authorities are coming.
“I’m very convinced that we’re very close to getting some of these things accomplished,” Pfluger said

articles.title: Ukrainian electronic warfare apparently knocked a Russian attack drone off course and into Lithuanian airspace, the country’s president says
articles.body:
Ukrainian electronic warfare apparently knocked a Russian attack drone off course and into Lithuanian airspace, the country’s president says
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said after a meeting of the State Defense Council that the drone shot down by NATO fighter jets over Lithuania on the night of September 15 was a Russian Gerbera drone.
Preliminary information indicates that the drone was intended to attack Ukraine but was thrown off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare systems and entered Lithuanian airspace, Nausėda said.
“Unfortunately, there may be more incidents like this in the future. The most important thing is for us to detect such drones in time — preferably while they are still over neighboring countries — so we can respond more quickly, since we really have very little time to prepare. Given our geographic position, Vilnius is not far from the border, and, of course, once such objects are detected, we could and should have the means to destroy drones or other aircraft.”
NATO fighter jets shot down the drone after it entered Lithuanian airspace on the night of September 15, marking the first time a drone had been destroyed over the country. The drone was downed between Kaunas and Kaišiadorys, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) northwest of Vilnius. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas later said the drone had been carrying an explosive device, which was rendered safe.
